The Administrator checks door alarms and monitoring devices, exits, fencing and staffing at the time of the event, and fixes any deficiency found within [24 hours]. If the facility can no longer meet the resident's safety needs, the Administrator follows ADM-04 and HLT-04.

Training and readiness: each resident's current photograph and physical description are kept in the record from admission, updated at least annually. All staff are trained on this policy at orientation (STF-03) and at least annually. The facility holds one missing-resident drill each year, and the Administrator documents it. Only the Administrator speaks to the media or the public about the event.

responsibilities.duty: Owns this policy; makes sure staff are trained; makes the DSS and ACLS notifications or confirms the SIC made them; reviews every event; completes post-event reassessment and corrective action.
Directs the search, makes the 911 call and the family notifications, assigns staff, and completes the incident report.
Report an absent resident at once, search the assigned area, keep other residents supervised, and document observations.
Checks alarms, doors, lighting and fencing after any event and repairs defects.

documentation: Incident report (INC-01) with search timeline and all notifications
Resident record note and post-event reassessment, with updated care plan and supervision plan
Sign-out log (VIS-01)
Current photograph and physical description in each resident record
Log of calls to the responsible person, county DSS and ACLS (name, date, time)
Annual missing-resident drill record and staff training sign-in sheets

policies.category: Identification and Supervision of Wandering Residents
policies.title: Identification, Assessment and Supervision of Wandering or Disoriented Residents; Door Alarms
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Home (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Home (10A NCAC 13G)
policies.purpose: To identify residents who are disoriented or who wander, to make sure staff report and assess changes in behavior, to provide a written individualized supervision plan for each such resident, and to make sure door alarms and other monitoring devices are tested and kept working.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] identifies disoriented or wandering residents at admission and continuously after admission. Staff report such behavior to the administrator or supervisor-in-charge. The facility assesses behavior changes, supervises these residents under a written plan and keeps door alarms and monitoring devices in working order. This policy meets 10A NCAC 13F .1211(7), .0305(h)(4) and .0901, and 10A NCAC 13G .0312 and .0901. Official item 5a, Reporting disoriented or wandering behavior to administration/SIC, is met by Procedures 3-4. Official item 5b, Identification and assessment of changes in behavior (wandering, increased confusion, etc.), is met by Procedures 1-2 and 5-6. Official item 5c, Facility's plan for supervision of disoriented or wandering residents, is met by Procedures 7-10, including the staffing requirement that applies to facilities with 7-12 residents. Official item 5d, Door alarms or other monitoring devices (operation and maintenance of), is met by Procedures 11-16. Where a facility has 7-12 residents, at least one staff member is awake at all times if any resident is disoriented or wanders, and the administrator or manager is on site or within 500 feet with two-way communication. [AGENCY NAME] keeps an awake staff member on every shift, including the 3rd shift (11:01 p.m.-7:00 a.m.), whenever any resident is disoriented or wanders, regardless of the number of residents.

definitions.definition: Walking or moving about without a clear purpose or safe destination, or trying to leave the building or a safe area without staff knowledge, including exit-seeking.
Confused about person, place, time or situation, so that the resident cannot reliably find the way, recognize hazards or protect himself or herself.
Direct observation of the resident's activities and the amount of oversight that is needed to keep the resident safe, as defined in 10A NCAC 13F .0102.
The administrator or the manager or designated staff member in charge of day-to-day operation when the administrator is absent.
A door alarm, chime, window alarm, bed or chair alarm, or other electronic or mechanical device that alerts staff when a resident moves toward or through an exit or leaves a bed or chair.

procedures: Identification at admission: during pre-admission screening (ADM-01) and the admission assessment (ADM-02), the admitting staff ask the resident, the responsible person and the physician about confusion, wandering, exit-seeking, getting lost and prior elopements. They review the FL-2 or other medical information. The results are recorded in the assessment.

Ongoing observation: every staff member watches for new or increased confusion, getting lost in the building, trying doors or windows, packing belongings, saying he or she needs to 'go home', night-time restlessness, following staff or visitors toward an exit, and sundowning. These are recorded on the shift notes.

Reporting by staff: any staff member who observes disoriented or wandering behavior, or a change in it, reports it verbally to the SIC immediately during the same shift. The staff member also documents the behavior in the resident's record the same shift (date, time, behavior and action taken).

Reporting to administration: the SIC reports new or worsening behavior to the Administrator by the end of the shift, or immediately if the resident left or attempted to leave the building. If the resident left the building or cannot be found, follow MIS-01.

Assessment of change: within 24 hours of a report, the Administrator or SIC observes the resident and reviews recent changes in medications, illness (for example, signs of infection), pain, hydration, sleep, environment and routine. The physician and responsible person are notified under HLT-03 when the change may signal a medical problem.

Reassessment: a documented change in behavior triggers a reassessment (ADM-02). The resident care plan (ADM-03) and the supervision plan below are updated promptly, with an interim supervision plan started on the same shift as the report.

Individual supervision plan: for each disoriented or wandering resident the facility keeps a written plan in the record. The plan states the level of supervision (for example, line-of-sight or checks at set intervals, and during which hours), the resident's room location, monitoring devices in use, planned activities and redirection strategies, identifiers such as a current photograph, and the rule that the resident goes off the premises only with an escort and is signed out (VIS-01).

Staffing: at least one staff member stays awake at all times when any resident is disoriented or wanders. In a facility with 7-12 residents the Administrator or manager must be on site or within 500 feet with two-way communication. The overall number of staff is set under STF-01. The Administrator adds staff when the supervision plans cannot be carried out safely.
Communication between shifts: the SIC tells each oncoming shift which residents are on a supervision plan and what changed. Changes are written on the shift report.

Limits of the facility: if the Administrator finds that the facility cannot keep the resident safe, even with added supervision, the Administrator follows ADM-04 and, if available, HLT-04. Physical restraints are not used to control wandering (RST-01).

Placement of devices: door alarms or other monitoring devices are placed on exits and other points as decided by the Administrator after assessing residents. A device never blocks or delays emergency exit and is installed and used in a way that complies with the fire safety requirements in FIR-01.

Testing: the Administrator assigns [MAINTENANCE STAFF] to test each door alarm and monitoring device at least weekly. The shift staff also confirm at the start of every shift that devices are on and working, and the batteries are changed on the manufacturer's schedule or sooner if low.

Response: every alarm is answered at once. A staff member goes to the exit, accounts for the resident who set it off and resets the device only after confirming everyone's whereabouts. Staff never disable, silence or cover a device to avoid alarms.

Malfunction: staff who find a device not working tell the SIC immediately. The SIC posts a staff member at the affected exit or increases checks until the device is repaired, and the Administrator has it repaired or replaced within [24 hours].

Maintenance log: each test, battery change, malfunction, repair and replacement is entered on the door alarm maintenance log with date, initials and results. The Administrator reviews the log monthly.

Training and review: all staff are trained on this policy at orientation (STF-03) and at least annually. The Administrator reviews every supervision plan at least quarterly and after any elopement attempt, incident or change in condition, and records the review in the record.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures identification, assessment, reassessment and supervision plans are completed; makes sure staffing meets the requirements for the facility's size; assigns door alarm testing and reviews the maintenance log.
Receives staff reports of wandering or disorientation, begins interim supervision, reports to the Administrator and notifies the physician and responsible person as required.
Observe, report and document behavior changes; carry out supervision plans; respond to alarms immediately.
Tests devices weekly, replaces batteries, completes the log and arranges repairs.

documentation: Admission assessment and reassessment records (ADM-02)
Resident care plan and individual written supervision plan
Shift notes and staff reports of disoriented or wandering behavior
Physician and responsible person notification records
Door alarm and monitoring device testing and maintenance log
Training sign-in sheets and quarterly plan review notes

policies.title: Fire Evacuation Plan, Fire Drills and Life Safety
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Home (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Home (10A NCAC 13G)
policies.purpose: To protect residents and staff from fire by keeping a written evacuation plan, holding unannounced fire drills on every shift, maintaining an automatically transmitting fire alarm system and complying with building and fire safety requirements.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written fire evacuation plan, conducts and documents drills and keeps its life safety systems in working order. Official item 6a, Copy of written fire evacuation plan, including where it will be posted in facility (10A NCAC 13G .0316; for adult care homes 10A NCAC 13F .0309), is met by Procedures 1-4. The plan includes a floor-plan diagram with evacuation routes and is posted at [POSTING LOCATIONS]. Official item 6b, Plan for fire drills/rehearsals and documentation of, is met by Procedures 5-10. Unannounced fire drills are held at least quarterly on each shift (1st 7:01 a.m.-3:00 p.m., 2nd 3:01 p.m.-11:00 p.m. and 3rd 11:01 p.m.-7:00 a.m.). Official item FCH-2.b(v), Life safety requirements (License a Family Care Home, Procedures step 2.b), is met by Procedures 11-17, including the fire alarm that transmits automatically to the local fire department dispatch center under 10A NCAC 13F .0307 and compliance with city and county fire safety requirements and with the physical plant requirements in 10A NCAC 13F .0301. For a family care home, the Administrator confirms the paragraph-level requirements of 10A NCAC 13G .0316 with ACLS and the county before licensure and keeps the written confirmation with this policy.

definitions.definition: A practice evacuation, conducted without advance notice to staff or residents, that tests the evacuation plan, the alarm and staff response.
A marked path from each resident room and area to an exit and a safe assembly point outside.
1st shift 7:01 a.m. to 3:00 p.m.; 2nd shift 3:01 p.m. to 11:00 p.m.; 3rd shift 11:01 p.m. to 7:00 a.m. (10A NCAC 13F .0102).
A company that receives alarm signals from the facility and relays them to the local fire department dispatch center.

procedures: The Administrator writes the fire evacuation plan for the building. It must contain a floor-plan diagram showing every room, exits, evacuation routes, fire extinguishers, pull stations and assembly points, and written steps for staff.

The plan states who sounds the alarm, who calls 911, who assists non-ambulatory residents and those with dementia, who closes doors, who takes the resident roster, who meets the fire department, and who accounts for each resident at the assembly point.

The plan is posted in [POSTING LOCATIONS], such as the entrance, each hallway and common areas. The posted diagram shows the 'You are here' location. The Administrator keeps a master copy in [LOCATION] and updates it whenever the layout or resident mobility needs change.
The Administrator reviews the plan at least annually, after every drill with problems and after any building alteration, and documents the review and the date.

Drill schedule: the Administrator schedules unannounced fire drills at least quarterly on each shift, varying the day, time and exit blocked. The drill is not announced in advance to the staff on duty or the residents.

During drills staff use the evacuation routes and practice the alarm, the 911 or alarm-company call and resident accounting. The drill also practices getting residents with limited mobility or cognitive impairment to a safe place, and tests alternate routes.

After each drill the Administrator or designee reviews the performance, records the time to complete evacuation and the problems found, and corrects problems promptly. Corrections are written on the drill record.

Every drill is recorded on the fire drill log: date, time, shift, how long the evacuation took, staff and residents participating, whether the alarm sounded, problems and corrective actions, and the signature of the person who conducted it.
The Administrator confirms before the end of each quarter that every shift has had a drill. A missed drill is made up immediately.

New staff are trained on the plan and shown the alarm, extinguishers, exits and routes during orientation, before working alone (STF-03). Staff are retrained at least annually and when the plan changes. Training is documented.

Fire alarm: the facility maintains a fire alarm system that transmits automatically to the local fire department dispatch center, directly or through a third-party monitoring service, as required by 10A NCAC 13F .0307. The Administrator keeps the contract or evidence of the connection and confirms the signal at installation and after repairs.

The alarm system, smoke detectors, emergency lighting and fire extinguishers are inspected, tested and maintained as required by the manufacturer, local code and the fire inspector. Each test and service is recorded and kept at the facility.

Local requirements: the Administrator complies with city and county fire safety requirements and schedules inspections by the local fire marshal as the authority requires. Inspection reports and corrections are kept on file.

Building and physical plant: new construction, additions, alterations and repairs must meet the physical plant requirements of 10A NCAC 13F .0300. An existing building meets the code in effect when it was licensed or altered. The Administrator does not begin alterations without checking requirements with DHSR, and any equivalency granted by DHSR is kept on file. Resident bedrooms are not placed on the second floor of certain pre-1984 two-story wood-frame adult care homes.
Egress: exits, corridors and stairways are kept free of obstructions at all times. Staff check exits daily. No door alarm or lock may keep a resident from leaving in a fire (WAN-01).

Discovery of fire: any person who sees smoke or fire sounds the alarm, helps residents closest to the fire to safety, closes doors, calls 911 if the alarm does not transmit, and follows the posted plan. Staff do not re-enter the building.

After any fire, alarm activation with response by the fire department, or evacuation, the Administrator documents it on an incident report (INC-01), notifies responsible persons and reports as required (REC-02). If residents are evacuated for emergencies, FIR-02 applies.

responsibilities.duty: Writes, posts and updates the plan; schedules drills; keeps the drill log and fire system records; coordinates with fire officials and DHSR.
Directs evacuation and accounts for all residents; conducts drills when assigned.
Know the plan, routes and equipment, take part in drills and keep exits clear.
Tests and maintains alarms, detectors, lighting and extinguishers and records the results.

documentation: Written fire evacuation plan with floor-plan diagram and evacuation routes
Record of where the plan is posted
Fire drill log (date, time, shift, evacuation time, participants, problems, corrective actions)
Fire alarm monitoring contract or documentation of connection to the dispatch center
Alarm, detector, extinguisher and emergency lighting inspection and service records
Local fire marshal inspection reports and DHSR equivalency or plan review approvals
Staff training records

policies.title: Disaster and Emergency Preparedness Plan
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Home (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Home (10A NCAC 13G)
policies.purpose: To prepare the facility to protect residents during fire, tornado, hurricane, power outage and other disasters or emergencies, including special needs sheltering, evacuation and transportation, and to meet reporting and visitation obligations during emergencies.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written disaster and emergency preparedness plan and keeps it in the facility. This policy meets official item 6c, Copy of written disaster plan (address minimum of fire, tornado, hurricane, and power outage), including plans for special needs sheltering and transportation during disasters (10A NCAC 13G .0316; for adult care homes 10A NCAC 13F .0309). The plan addresses at least fire, tornado, hurricane and power outage, plus special needs sheltering and transportation during disasters. The facility uses the North Carolina Risk Management Portal Licensed Care Facility Risk Management Plan template (https://rmp.nc.gov/portal/#) to write the plan. If residents are evacuated, the Administrator reports to local emergency management, the county DSS and ACLS within 4 hours of the decision to evacuate and again within 4 hours of the residents' return. Residents keep visitation rights during a disaster declaration or emergency as provided by N.C.G.S. 131D-7.2 and the visitation protocols the Secretary of DHHS establishes under N.C.G.S. 131D-7.1.

definitions.definition: An event such as fire, tornado, hurricane, flood, power outage, severe weather, loss of water or heat, infectious disease outbreak or other event that threatens resident health or safety or disrupts normal operation.
A shelter operated by local authorities for persons who need medical or personal care support and cannot use a general population shelter.
The Administrator's or SIC's decision, or an official order, to move residents out of the facility.
The plan created through the NC Risk Management Portal Licensed Care Facility template.

procedures: The Administrator completes the facility's Licensed Care Facility Risk Management Plan in the NC Risk Management Portal (rmp.nc.gov/portal) before the facility is licensed. The plan is printed and kept in the facility in [LOCATION] where all staff can find it, and a copy is kept off-site by [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].

The plan includes, at minimum, procedures for fire, tornado, hurricane and power outage, and also covers flooding, winter storms, water or heat loss and loss of communications. Each section lists who does what, what supplies are needed and when to act.
The plan identifies the facility's location in local hazard zones and evacuation zones, and the local emergency management contact [PHONE], the county DSS contact [PHONE] and ACLS (919-855-3765).

Special needs sheltering: the Administrator contacts local emergency management each year to learn the special needs shelter criteria and registration steps. Residents who are likely to qualify are identified and registered if required. The plan states which residents will go to which shelter or host facility.

Transportation: the plan names the vehicles, drivers or transport contractors [VENDOR AND PHONE] to be used to move residents. It states how wheelchair-dependent and bedbound residents will be moved, with a back-up if the primary transportation is not available. Agreements are in writing and are reviewed annually.

The plan lists each resident's medications, diet, equipment, oxygen needs, cognitive status and responsible person. The resident roster, medication administration records, medications, face sheets, advance directive information (RR-03) and a supply kit are ready to travel with residents.

Supply readiness: the facility keeps a minimum of [3] days of drinking water, non-perishable food meeting therapeutic diet needs (NUT-01), flashlights, batteries, a battery or hand-crank radio, first aid supplies, hygiene and incontinence supplies, and a back-up power plan for essential equipment such as oxygen concentrators and refrigerated medications.

Power outage: staff use flashlights, not candles. The SIC calls the utility, protects medications that need refrigeration, relocates residents on oxygen concentrators to back-up oxygen and assesses heat and cold risk. If the outage cannot be fixed safely, the Administrator decides whether to evacuate.

Severe weather: during a tornado warning, staff move residents to the pre-identified safe area away from windows. During a hurricane or flood watch or warning, the Administrator reviews the plan, decides whether to shelter in place or evacuate, and informs responsible persons.

Staff assignments: the plan assigns an emergency role to every staff member. The Administrator keeps a staff call list and has a plan to bring in more staff. Staff are trained on the plan at orientation (STF-03) and at least annually. A tabletop or practice exercise is done at least once a year and recorded.

Evacuation decision and reporting: when the Administrator or SIC decides to evacuate residents, whether by official order or the facility's own decision, a report is made within 4 hours of the decision to local emergency management, the county DSS and ACLS. The report states the reason, the number of residents, where they are going and a contact number.

Return report: within 4 hours of the residents' return to the facility, the Administrator again reports to local emergency management, the county DSS and ACLS. Each report is recorded with the date, time, person called and information given.

During evacuation, staff take the roster, keep a log of each resident's location, continue medication administration and personal care, keep residents with their belongings and mobility aids where possible, and notify each responsible person of the resident's location as soon as practical.

Visitation: residents' visitation rights continue during a disaster declaration or emergency under N.C.G.S. 131D-7.2. The Administrator follows the visitation protocols established by the Secretary under N.C.G.S. 131D-7.1 and posts them. Any safety measure the facility uses must comply with those protocols and must not take away a resident's right to visits. See also VIS-01.

After the event the Administrator conducts a debrief within 7 days, records what worked and what did not, corrects the plan and records the changes. Any injury, death or damage is handled under INC-01, HLT-08 and REC-02.

The Administrator reviews and updates the plan at least annually, when the building, population or contacts change, and after any activation. The date of each review is recorded and the updated plan is placed in the facility.

responsibilities.duty: Prepares and updates the plan, arranges shelter and transportation agreements, decides whether to evacuate, makes the 4-hour reports and leads the debrief.
Carries out the plan when the Administrator is absent, including notifications and resident accounting.
Know their emergency roles, take part in training and exercises and follow instructions during an emergency.
Maintains generators, flashlights, emergency supplies and utility shutoffs.

documentation: Written disaster plan (NC Risk Management Portal Licensed Care Facility Risk Management Plan) kept in the facility
Special needs shelter registration or correspondence with local emergency management
Transportation agreements and vendor contact list
Evacuation reports to local emergency management, county DSS and ACLS (decision and return), with time and person contacted
Resident location log during evacuation
Emergency exercise and training records
Post-event debrief notes and plan revisions

policies.category: Infection Control Procedures in Accordance with CDC Guidelines and Session Law 2011-99
policies.title: Standard Precautions, Hand Hygiene and Glove Use
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Home (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Home (10A NCAC 13G)
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection to residents, staff and visitors by defining Standard Precautions and giving staff clear instructions on handwashing and glove use.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows CDC guidelines and the infection control requirements of Session Law 2011-99, and applies Standard Precautions to the care of all residents at all times, regardless of known or suspected infection. This policy meets 10A NCAC 13G .1211 (and 10A NCAC 13F .1211(4) for adult care homes) and the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030. Official item 7j, Definition of and use of Standard Precautions, is met by the definitions and Procedures 1-3. Official item 7k, Policy on handwashing, instructions for staff (how and when to handwash), is met by Procedures 4-8. Official item 7l, Policy on use of gloves, instructions for staff (when to use and how to properly remove), is met by Procedures 9-14. Related infection control items are addressed in INF-02 (bloodborne pathogens, sharps and exposures), INF-03 (sanitation and compliance monitoring) and INF-04 (outbreaks).

definitions.definition: The basic infection prevention practices used with every resident: hand hygiene; gloves, gowns, masks and eye protection when exposure is possible; respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette; safe handling of sharps; cleaning and disinfection of equipment and surfaces; safe handling of linen and waste; and prompt cleanup of spills. They treat all blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions (except sweat), non-intact skin and mucous membranes as possibly infectious.
Washing hands with soap and water or cleaning them with an alcohol-based hand rub that contains at least 60 percent alcohol.
Gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection and face shields used to protect staff and residents from contact with infectious material.
Hands with dirt, blood, body fluids or other material that can be seen.

procedures: Standard Precautions are used for every resident, at every contact, on every shift. Staff do not decide to apply them based on the resident's diagnosis or appearance.

Staff choose PPE based on the task. They use gloves for contact with blood, body fluids, mucous membranes, non-intact skin or contaminated equipment. They use a gown, mask and eye protection when splashes or sprays are likely. Staff cover coughs and sneezes, and residents and visitors with symptoms are offered a mask and tissues and hand hygiene supplies.

The Administrator or infection control designee (INF-03) makes sure PPE, soap, paper towels and alcohol-based hand rub are always stocked and placed where care is given, and that staff are trained on this policy at orientation (STF-03) and annually.

When to wash hands: staff perform hand hygiene when they arrive and before leaving; before and after direct contact with a resident; before and after assisting with meals or medications; before handling food; after toileting or assisting with toileting; after contact with body fluids; after touching soiled linen, trash or contaminated surfaces; after sneezing, coughing or blowing the nose; after using the restroom; and always immediately after removing gloves.

Use soap and water, not hand rub, when hands are visibly soiled, after contact with a resident who has diarrhea or suspected or confirmed Clostridioides difficile or norovirus, and before eating. Alcohol-based hand rub may be used in other situations when hands are not visibly soiled.

How to wash with soap and water: (1) remove rings and watches if possible, and keep nails short and clean; (2) wet hands with clean running water; (3) apply soap; (4) rub palms, backs of hands, between fingers, under nails and wrists for at least 20 seconds; (5) rinse thoroughly with running water; (6) dry with a clean paper towel; (7) turn off the faucet with the towel; (8) discard the towel.

How to use alcohol-based hand rub: apply the amount recommended by the manufacturer to the palm of one hand, and rub hands together covering all surfaces, including fingertips, between fingers and thumbs, until completely dry. This should take about 20 seconds. Do not wipe or rinse the product off.

Staff with open cuts, sores or dermatitis on the hands cover them with a waterproof bandage and gloves, and tell the Administrator if the condition prevents proper hand hygiene. Staff who have a communicable illness follow INF-05 and INF-04 on staying away from work.

Gloves are required whenever contact with blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions, mucous membranes, non-intact skin, wounds, soiled linen or contaminated surfaces is expected. Examples are perineal care, toileting, ostomy, incontinence care, wound care, oral care, finger-stick glucose testing, handling soiled items and cleaning spills.

Gloves are single use. Staff put on clean gloves right before the task, check that they are intact and the correct size, and wear them only for one resident and one task. Staff change gloves between residents and between tasks on the same resident (for example, from perineal care to face care) and when gloves are torn or heavily soiled.
Never wash and reuse disposable gloves. Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene: staff always perform hand hygiene before putting on gloves and immediately after removing them.

How to remove gloves: (1) with one gloved hand, grasp the outside of the other glove near the wrist; (2) peel it off, turning it inside out, and hold it in the remaining gloved hand; (3) slide the fingers of the bare hand under the cuff of the remaining glove; (4) peel it off over the first glove, inside out, so that both gloves are enclosed; (5) discard in the trash (in a biohazard bag if saturated with blood or body fluids); (6) perform hand hygiene.
Staff who are allergic to latex use latex-free gloves, which the facility provides at no cost. Non-latex gloves are stocked in sizes to fit all staff.
Gloves are removed before touching clean surfaces such as door handles, charts, phones, medication carts and the refrigerator. Staff do not wear gloves in hallways or between tasks.

The Administrator or designee observes hand hygiene and glove use at least [monthly], documents the observations, retrains staff when needed and reports results to QA (GOV-04). Violations of this policy are handled under STF-04.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts and enforces this policy; ensures supplies and training; monitors compliance.
Stocks PPE and hand hygiene supplies, observes practice, and reports findings (INF-03).
Apply Standard Precautions, perform hand hygiene and use and remove gloves as taught.
Residents are encouraged and helped to wash hands; visitors follow posted hand hygiene and respiratory etiquette instructions.

documentation: Training sign-in sheets and competency checklists for hand hygiene and glove use
Hand hygiene and glove observation records
PPE and hand hygiene supply inventory
Posted handwashing and glove removal instructions

policies.category: Infection Control Procedures in Accordance with CDC Guidelines and Session Law 2011-99
policies.title: Bloodborne Pathogens, Sharps Disposal and Staff Exposure Response
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Home (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Home (10A NCAC 13G)
policies.purpose: To protect residents and staff from bloodborne pathogens such as HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C by setting rules for sharps disposal, disinfection of reusable resident care items, blood and body fluid precautions and the steps to take after a staff exposure.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows CDC guidelines and Session Law 2011-99, and complies with the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030, and 10A NCAC 13G .1211 (and 10A NCAC 13F .1211(4) for adult care homes). Official item 7a, Proper disposal of single-use equipment used to puncture skin, mucous membranes and other tissues, and proper disinfection of reusable resident care items used for multiple residents, is met by Procedures 1-8. Official item 7d, Blood and bodily fluid precautions, is met by Procedures 9-13. Official item 7e, Procedures to be followed when adult care home staff is exposed to blood or other body fluids of another person in a manner that poses a significant risk of transmission of HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C or other bloodborne pathogens, is met by Procedures 14-20. Standard Precautions, hand hygiene and gloves are covered in INF-01.

definitions.definition: Microorganisms in human blood or certain body fluids that can cause disease, including HIV, hepatitis B virus and hepatitis C virus.
Any single-use item that can puncture or cut skin, mucous membranes or other tissue, such as needles, lancets, pen-needle tips, razors and syringes, and broken glass contaminated with blood.

A needlestick or cut with a contaminated sharp, a splash of blood or body fluid to the eyes, nose or mouth, a bite that breaks the skin, or contact of blood or body fluid with non-intact skin, in a manner that poses a significant risk of transmission.

An item used for more than one resident, such as a glucometer, blood pressure cuff, thermometer, wheelchair, shower chair, lift sling or other equipment, that must be cleaned and disinfected between residents.
The person whose blood or body fluid was involved in an exposure.

procedures: Single-use sharps (needles, lancets, pen needles, syringes and similar items) are never reused. Used sharps are discarded immediately after use, at the point of use, into a rigid, puncture-resistant, leak-proof, labeled sharps container. Sharps containers are within easy reach of where sharps are used and are kept upright.

Staff never recap, bend, break or shear needles by hand, never carry loose sharps and never reach into a sharps container. Containers are replaced when three-quarters full. Full containers are closed tightly and disposed of through [LICENSED MEDICAL WASTE VENDOR] or another method that complies with North Carolina medical waste rules.
Finger-stick lancets used for residents are single-use, auto-disabling devices. A lancing device must never be used on more than one resident unless it is a single-use disposable device.

Reusable resident care items used for more than one resident, including glucometers, are cleaned and disinfected between each resident. Staff use an EPA-registered disinfectant that is labeled for the intended use (for a blood glucose meter, the product the manufacturer recommends) and follow the label for contact time.
Staff wear gloves when cleaning and disinfecting. Items that cannot be disinfected between residents are assigned to one resident. Items visibly soiled with blood are cleaned first, then disinfected.
The infection control designee (INF-03) keeps a list of reusable items, the disinfectant used and the cleaning steps, and trains staff on them.
Staff who handle sharps are trained at orientation (STF-03) and at least annually on proper use and disposal and on the exposure steps in this policy.

The Administrator keeps a record of sharps containers' disposal and orders supplies so that containers and safety devices are always available. Where safer devices are available for the facility's sharps, they are used.

Blood and body fluid precautions: staff treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious and use Standard Precautions (INF-01) for every resident. They wear gloves for any contact with blood, body fluids or non-intact skin, and wear a gown, mask and eye protection when splashing is possible.

Spill cleanup: staff put on gloves, remove visible material with absorbent towels, clean the area with soap and water, then disinfect with an EPA-registered disinfectant (or a freshly made 1:10 bleach solution if the product is appropriate for the surface), following label contact times. Soiled material is bagged and placed in the trash. If material is saturated and would drip, it is placed in a labeled biohazard bag. Hands are washed afterward.
Soiled linen is handled as little as possible, bagged where used and not shaken or rinsed in resident areas. Staff wear gloves when handling it (DLV-01).
Staff cover any cuts or open skin with a waterproof dressing. Staff do not eat, drink, apply cosmetics or handle contact lenses in areas where blood or body fluids may be present.

The Administrator offers the hepatitis B vaccine, at no cost to the employee, to every staff member whose duties could result in contact with blood or body fluids, within 10 working days of starting those duties. A staff member may decline and sign a declination form and may accept the vaccine later.

Exposure response, first aid: a staff member who has an exposure immediately stops the task and, for a needlestick, cut or splash to skin, washes the area with soap and water. For eyes, nose or mouth, flush with clean water or saline for several minutes. Do not squeeze the wound, scrub or use bleach or caustic agents.

Reporting: the staff member immediately reports the exposure to the SIC and the Administrator. The SIC makes sure the resident or other person receives needed care and the incident is documented on an incident report (INC-01) the same shift. The report states the date, time, place, task, device involved, body part exposed and the source person's identity if known.

Medical evaluation: the exposed staff member is sent immediately, and no later than within 2 hours if possible, to [OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH CLINIC OR EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT, ADDRESS, PHONE] for evaluation. Treatment, including post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV when it is recommended, works best when started promptly. The Administrator sends the clinic the incident report and the source person's information that is available.

Source person: the Administrator asks the source person (or the legal representative) to consent to testing for HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C as allowed by North Carolina law. Test results are shared only with the exposed person's health care provider and are kept confidential (RR-04). If the source person refuses or cannot consent, the clinic is told and follows state law and its own protocols.

Follow-up: the exposed staff member receives the health care provider's written opinion and follow-up testing, counseling and treatment as recommended. The employer pays the costs of the evaluation and follow-up related to a work exposure, in compliance with 29 CFR 1910.1030.

Records: the Administrator keeps a confidential exposure record, separate from the personnel file, for each exposed employee, and keeps it for the length of employment plus 30 years as required by 29 CFR 1910.1030. A sharps injury log is kept without the names of employees.

Review: within 7 days the Administrator reviews each exposure to find the cause, corrects the problem (for example, device, practice or training) and reports to QA (GOV-04). If the event involved an outbreak or reportable disease, INF-04 also applies.

responsibilities.duty: Provides sharps containers, safer devices, vaccination and exposure care; keeps records; investigates each exposure.
Takes the first report, assures care of the exposed person and the source person, and completes the incident report.
Maintains the list of reusable items and disinfection steps, and trains staff.
Dispose of sharps properly, apply blood and body fluid precautions, disinfect shared items and report exposures at once.

documentation: Training records for bloodborne pathogens and sharps
Sharps container disposal records
List of reusable resident care items and disinfection schedule
Hepatitis B vaccination offer, acceptance or declination forms
Incident report for each exposure and confidential exposure record, and sharps injury log
Health care provider's written opinion and follow-up records (kept confidentially)

policies.category: Infection Control Procedures in Accordance with CDC Guidelines and Session Law 2011-99
policies.title: Sanitation, Supplies, Infection Control Designee and Compliance Monitoring
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Home (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Home (10A NCAC 13G): all staff, contracted workers and volunteers
policies.purpose: To keep resident rooms, common areas and shared equipment clean and disinfected. To make sure infection control supplies are always available to staff. To keep staff with infectious skin conditions away from residents. To name the person who directs infection control. To check regularly that this policy is followed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows CDC infection control guidelines and the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030). This policy meets 10A NCAC 13G .1211 as follows. Item 7b (Sanitation of rooms and equipment, including cleaning procedures, agents and schedules) is met by Procedures 1-6. Item 7c (Accessibility of infection control devices and supplies) is met by Procedures 7-8. Item 7f (Staff with exudative lesions or weeping dermatitis) is met by Procedures 9-11. Item 7h (Designated on-site staff member knowledgeable about CDC guidelines) is met by Procedures 12-13. Item 7g (Procedure for monitoring compliance) is met by Procedures 14-17. Related infection control topics are in INF-01, INF-02, INF-04 and INF-05.

definitions.definition: A skin sore, wound, rash or infection that drains or oozes fluid (pus, serum or blood) and may contaminate hands, equipment or surfaces.
A hospital-grade disinfectant registered with the U.S. EPA. It is used exactly as the label directs, including the wet contact time.
A surface touched often by many people, such as doorknobs, handrails, light switches, call devices, faucet handles, remote controls and dining table edges.
The on-site staff member appointed in writing to direct infection control activities and train staff.
Equipment used for more than one resident, such as blood pressure cuffs, thermometers, wheelchairs, shower chairs, lifts and glucometers.

procedures: Housekeeping staff clean and disinfect each resident room daily. This includes floors, bed rails, bedside tables, call devices, door handles and bathroom fixtures. Staff clean from cleanest to dirtiest areas and use a fresh cloth or mop head for each room.

Staff clean toilets, sinks, showers and tubs at least daily and after any visible soiling. Staff clean and disinfect high-touch surfaces in common areas (dining room, living room, hallways, handrails) at least [NUMBER] times daily and whenever soiled. The schedule is posted in the housekeeping closet and initialed by the person who completes each task.

Staff use only an EPA-registered disinfectant that is approved by the Administrator and used per label directions. Surfaces are cleaned of visible soil first, then kept wet for the full label contact time. Staff keep safety data sheets for all chemicals where staff can reach them. Chemicals are never mixed.

Staff clean and disinfect shared equipment between residents and after each use. They wipe thermometers, blood pressure cuffs, stethoscopes, shower chairs, commodes, lifts and wheelchairs. Fingerstick lancing devices are never shared between residents. A glucometer is used only per the manufacturer's disinfection instructions or is assigned to one resident.

Staff clean spills of blood or body fluids right away. They wear gloves and other PPE, remove visible material with absorbent towels, then disinfect the area with an EPA-registered disinfectant labeled for bloodborne pathogens. Alternatively, they use a freshly made 1:10 bleach-and-water solution. Contaminated materials go into a leak-proof bag or regulated waste container per INF-02.

Staff handle soiled linen as little as possible. They bag it at the point of use, wear gloves, and do not rinse or sort it in resident areas. They wash linen in hot water with detergent and dry it fully (see DLV-01). Clean and soiled linen are stored and carried separately. The Housekeeping Supervisor or the Administrator, if there is no supervisor, reviews cleaning and laundry logs weekly.

The Administrator makes sure the following are always stocked: gloves in all sizes, alcohol-based hand rub, soap and paper towels, gowns, masks, eye protection, sharps containers, disinfectant wipes and spray, biohazard bags, spill kits, and thermometers. Staff check and restock these supplies weekly.

Supplies are kept in [LOCATION OF INFECTION CONTROL SUPPLY STATION] and are not locked away from staff. Gloves and alcohol-based hand rub are also placed at [LOCATIONS, e.g., each hallway, medication area, kitchen entry and each bathroom]. Sharps containers are located in [LOCATION]. This location list is posted in the staff area and reviewed with each new employee at orientation. Staff tell the Infection Control Designee immediately if any item runs low.
Staff must tell the Administrator or the person in charge before starting a shift if they have any skin lesion or dermatitis that is draining, oozing or weeping. Staff may not wait to be asked.

A staff member with an exudative lesion or weeping dermatitis is not allowed to give direct resident care in which the resident, equipment or devices could contact the lesion or dermatitis. This restriction stays in place until the condition has resolved. The Administrator or person in charge decides, with the staff member's healthcare provider's guidance if needed, when the condition has resolved. The Administrator documents the start and end dates.

During the restriction, the staff member may do tasks that do not involve contact between the lesion and residents, equipment, devices, food or clean supplies, if work is available and the lesion can be fully covered. The Administrator records the restriction in the employee health section of the personnel record. The Administrator arranges replacement coverage so that staffing levels in STF-01 are met.

The Administrator appoints in writing an on-site staff member to be the Infection Control Designee. The name is [INFECTION CONTROL DESIGNEE NAME], title [TITLE]. This person must be knowledgeable about the CDC guidelines on infection control. A backup designee is named for periods of absence.

The Infection Control Designee directs infection control activities and makes sure all staff are trained in this policy and in INF-01 to INF-05. Training occurs at orientation before the staff member gives resident care (see STF-03), then at least annually, and whenever the policy changes or an audit shows a gap. Training is documented with date, topic, trainer and staff signature. The Designee keeps current on CDC guidance at [CDC WEBSITE OR OTHER SOURCE].

The Infection Control Designee observes staff practice each month. This includes hand hygiene, glove use, equipment cleaning, laundry handling, sharps handling and PPE use. The Designee records findings on the Infection Control Audit Checklist.

The Designee also checks that cleaning logs are complete, supplies are stocked and accessible, and employee lesion restrictions are documented. The Designee reviews resident infections, such as respiratory, GI, skin and urinary tract infections, for patterns each month.

When an audit finds a gap, the Designee corrects it on the spot when possible and retrains the staff member. The Designee records the corrective action and a re-check date, and the Administrator signs the checklist within 5 business days.

The Administrator reviews audit results at least quarterly. Results are included in the quality assurance review described in GOV-04. Audit checklists, logs and training records are kept [NUMBER] years and are available to the surveyor on request.

responsibilities.duty: Approves products and schedules, funds and stocks supplies, appoints the Infection Control Designee, manages employee lesion restrictions, and reviews audit results.
Directs infection control, trains staff, performs monthly audits, tracks resident infections and recommends corrective action.
Perform scheduled cleaning, use disinfectants per label, and document completed tasks.
Clean shared equipment between residents, use PPE, restock supplies and report their own lesions or dermatitis before the shift.

documentation: Cleaning and disinfection schedule and completed logs
Infection control supply location list and weekly stock check
Safety data sheets for cleaning chemicals
Infection Control Designee appointment letter
Infection control training records
Employee lesion/dermatitis restriction record
Monthly Infection Control Audit Checklists with corrective actions

policies.category: Infection Control Procedures in Accordance with CDC Guidelines and Session Law 2011-99
policies.title: Communicable Disease Outbreak Reporting and COVID-19 Protocols
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Home (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Home (10A NCAC 13G): all staff, residents, visitors and contracted providers
policies.purpose: To make sure a suspected communicable disease outbreak is recognized quickly, reported to the local health department by a named person, and controlled. To set the facility's COVID-19 protocols for screening, isolation, testing, visitation and reporting.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] reports suspected communicable disease outbreaks to the local health department and follows the health department's directions. This policy meets 10A NCAC 13G .1211 item 7i (Procedure for reporting suspected communicable disease outbreaks to the local health department and who is responsible for doing so) through Procedures 1-8. The Administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], is responsible for reporting. If the Administrator is unavailable, the designated Manager-in-Charge or the Infection Control Designee reports. It also meets item 7n (COVID-19 Protocols) through Procedures 9-18. All protocols are kept in line with current CDC and NC DHHS guidance. The Infection Control Designee checks that guidance at least monthly and whenever it changes, and updates this policy as needed.

definitions.definition: Two or more residents or staff with the same new illness (for example vomiting, diarrhea, fever, cough or rash) within a short period. It also includes one case of a disease the health department considers urgent, or any cluster the staff cannot explain.
The county health department for the county where the facility is located: [LOCAL HEALTH DEPARTMENT NAME], phone [PHONE], after-hours [PHONE].
Separating a resident who is sick or infected from others (private room, door closed when possible, PPE for staff) for the time current guidance specifies.
Contact with a person with a communicable disease that meets the current CDC or NC DHHS definition for exposure.

procedures: All staff watch residents each shift for new symptoms of infection (fever, cough, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, new confusion, sore throat). They report them immediately to the person in charge, who records them on the Daily Infection Surveillance Log. The log shows resident name, room, symptoms, onset date and action taken.

The person in charge reviews the log every shift. If two or more people have similar symptoms, or any single case appears serious or unusual, the person in charge calls the Administrator right away, including nights and weekends.

The Administrator, or the Manager-in-Charge if the Administrator cannot be reached, calls the local health department the same day the outbreak is suspected. The person reporting does not wait for lab confirmation.

The reporter gives the health department the number of ill residents and staff, symptoms, onset dates, units or rooms affected, any testing done and the control steps already taken. The reporter records the name of the health department contact, date, time and instructions on the Outbreak Report Form.
The Administrator follows the health department's directions on isolation, testing, cohorting, visitation limits and admissions. The Administrator posts the directions for staff.

The Administrator notifies each affected resident's responsible person, family or legal representative and the resident's physician. The Administrator also notifies the Adult Care Licensure Section at 919-855-3765 if the health department or ACLS directs this or if the situation affects the facility's ability to meet resident needs. Notices are recorded with date, time and name of person contacted.

The Infection Control Designee directs control measures. These include Standard Precautions and transmission-based precautions as indicated, extra cleaning and disinfection of high-touch surfaces, hand hygiene reminders and PPE supplies at the point of care. The Designee tracks new cases daily until the health department declares the outbreak over.

The Administrator keeps the Outbreak Report Form, line list, health department communications and notifications. After the outbreak ends, the Administrator completes a written review of what worked, what did not and any changes needed, and shares it with the Quality Assurance review in GOV-04.

Screening: Staff and essential visitors are screened for symptoms and known exposure before entering the building when community transmission or health department guidance calls for it. Anyone with symptoms or a recent exposure per current guidance does not enter or work, and must follow the return-to-work or return-to-visit rules in current guidance. Residents are checked for symptoms at least daily during any outbreak or when guidance requires, and are checked right away when symptoms appear.

Testing: A resident with COVID-19 symptoms is tested promptly, either with a test on site or through the resident's physician or the health department. During an outbreak or after an exposure, the Administrator follows the health department's testing plan for residents and staff. Results are recorded in the resident's record or the employee health file.

Isolation: A resident who tests positive or is suspected to have COVID-19 is moved to a private room, if available, and stays there for the period required by current CDC and NC DHHS guidance. Staff use the PPE required by current guidance, which includes a fitted mask or respirator, eye protection, gown and gloves. Meals and activities are provided in the room when needed. Staff keep supervision and personal care in place so that the resident's needs continue to be met.

Staff exposed or ill: Staff with COVID-19 stay out of work for the period required by current guidance. The Administrator arranges staffing coverage so that STF-01 levels are kept. Staff who return follow the masking and other rules in current guidance.

Vaccination and prevention: The facility offers residents and staff education about COVID-19, influenza and other recommended vaccines and documents each person's acceptance or declination. The facility keeps masks, tests, hand rub and PPE on hand (see INF-03).

Visitation: The facility allows visitation consistent with G.S. 131D-7.1 and 131D-7.2 and current NC DHHS visitation guidance. During a COVID-19 outbreak, the Administrator may add precautions such as masking, screening or visiting in the resident's room, but does not end visits entirely unless a legal order requires it. Compassionate care and end-of-life visits are always permitted with precautions. See VIS-01.

Communication: The Administrator tells residents, staff and responsible persons when a case or outbreak occurs. The notice describes the situation in general terms without naming other residents, protects privacy under RR-04, and explains precautions and visitation changes.

Reporting: The Administrator reports COVID-19 cases and outbreaks to the local health department as in Procedures 3-4. The Administrator also makes any additional reports NC DHHS requires, and records the date, method and person who made each report.

When guidance changes, the Infection Control Designee updates the protocols and trains staff before the change takes effect, or within 3 days if the change is immediate. Training is documented in the training records.

responsibilities.duty: Reports suspected outbreaks to the local health department, notifies responsible persons and physicians, and implements health department directions. The Manager-in-Charge acts as the backup reporter.
Reviews surveillance logs, directs control measures, tracks CDC and NC DHHS guidance and updates the protocols.
Reviews the surveillance log, escalates suspected outbreaks immediately and starts isolation and PPE measures.
Report symptoms in residents and in themselves, follow isolation and PPE rules, and stay home when ill.

documentation: Daily Infection Surveillance Log
Outbreak Report Form and line list
Health department call record and written instructions
Notifications to families, responsible persons, physicians and ACLS
COVID-19 screening, testing and isolation records
Vaccine acceptance/declination records
Staff training records for protocol changes
After-outbreak review

policies.category: Infection Control Procedures in Accordance with CDC Guidelines and Session Law 2011-99
policies.title: Tuberculosis Screening (Two-Step) and Employee Health
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Home (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Home (10A NCAC 13G): all residents, employees, contracted staff and volunteers with resident contact
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of tuberculosis (TB) by screening residents and staff using two-step testing. To define the testing process, follow-up of results, and employee health records.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] tests every resident and staff member for TB using the two-step method. Staff are tested before they work with residents, and residents are tested at admission. This policy meets 10A NCAC 13G .1211 item 7m (policy and process for completing two-step TB testing of residents and staff) and rule .0405 through Procedures 1-18. Residents' TB testing, medical examination and immunization documentation also follows 10A NCAC 13F .0703 as covered in Procedures 6-8. The Infection Control Designee tracks the testing and the Administrator makes sure no one starts work or is admitted without the required documentation.

definitions.definition: A first tuberculin skin test (TST) read 48-72 hours after placement. If the first result is negative, a second TST is placed 1-3 weeks later and read 48-72 hours after placement. The second step finds people whose first reaction was missed or was too small (the 'booster effect').
A skin test reaction at or above the size cut-off for the person's risk group under CDC guidance, or a positive blood test (IGRA). It requires symptom screening and a chest X-ray.
Interferon-gamma release assay, a TB blood test that may be used in place of a skin test when the physician or health department approves.

definitions.term: Latent TB infection / active TB disease
definitions.definition: Latent infection has no symptoms and is not contagious. Active disease can be contagious and requires medical treatment and health department involvement.

procedures: The Administrator checks TB documentation before any new hire starts duty and before any resident is admitted. No employee works with residents without Step 1 completed and read. No resident is admitted without the required TB documentation.

Staff: A new employee provides written results of a documented two-step TB test, or documented proof of a previous two-step negative result or a prior positive result with chest X-ray results, as accepted by the rule. If none exists, the employee gets Step 1 through [CLINIC / PROVIDER NAME] on or before the first day, and the facility has the result read 48-72 hours later.

If the Step 1 result is negative, the employee must get Step 2 1-3 weeks after Step 1. The result is read in 48-72 hours. The Infection Control Designee tracks the due date on the TB Tracking Log. Step 2 is completed within the time required by rule .0405.

If an employee or resident has a positive test, a chest X-ray and symptom screen by a physician or the health department are required before the person works or is admitted. The person may not work or be admitted until a physician states in writing that the person is free from active TB disease. The facility follows the health department's directions.

Employees with a previous positive result do not repeat skin testing. Each year they complete a TB symptom screen and report symptoms right away. The Designee records the screening on the employee health record.

Residents: The resident's physician completes TB testing at or before admission, and the results are part of the admission medical documentation. Where no documented two-step result is available, the facility has Step 1 placed and read, and Step 2 completed 1-3 weeks later, within the time frame in rule .0405.

The resident's admission documentation must also show the medical examination and the immunization status required by 10A NCAC 13F .0703. The Administrator reviews the documents against the Admission Checklist before admission and records the date reviewed.

A resident whose test is positive needs a chest X-ray and the physician's written statement that the resident is free from active TB before admission. If symptoms of active TB appear, the facility acts under Procedure 12.

The Administrator offers each resident and employee information about recommended vaccines, including influenza and COVID-19 vaccines, and records acceptance or declination in the resident record or the employee health record.
Each year, the facility reviews the TB risk of the building and its population. The Designee records any local health department TB alerts.

Staff and residents are screened for TB symptoms (cough lasting 3 weeks or more, bloody sputum, night sweats, fever, unexplained weight loss) at a regular interval that the Administrator sets in writing, and any time symptoms appear.

Anyone with symptoms of active TB is separated from others, wears a mask, and is referred to a physician the same day. The Administrator notifies the local health department right away and follows its directions (see INF-04). Staff with symptoms do not work until medically cleared.

The Infection Control Designee maintains the TB Tracking Log showing each person's name, role, Step 1 and Step 2 dates, results, X-ray dates and next due screening. The Designee reviews the log monthly.

The Administrator reviews the log with the Designee each month. Overdue items are followed up within 2 business days. A resident or employee overdue for required testing is handled according to rule .0405, and the corrective action is documented.

Employee health: Each employee's personnel file has a health section that includes TB results, immunization or declination forms, and any restriction records (see INF-03). It is kept separate from other personnel information and is confidential.
Records for staff and residents are kept in line with REC-01 and STF-02, and are made available to the surveyor on request.
Test results and health information are shared only with people who need them to protect health and safety. They are handled as confidential under RR-04.
The Infection Control Designee trains all staff annually on TB signs and symptoms, transmission, testing requirements and how to report concerns.

responsibilities.duty: Confirms TB documentation before hire and admission, enforces exclusion of anyone not cleared, and reviews the Tracking Log monthly.
Maintains the TB Tracking Log, schedules Step 2 and annual screenings, and trains staff.
Performs and reads tests, orders chest X-rays and documents clearance.
Provide TB results on time, report symptoms and follow restrictions.

documentation: TB Tracking Log
Two-step TB test results for each employee and resident
Chest X-ray and physician clearance letters
Annual symptom screening records
Resident admission medical and immunization documentation
Vaccine acceptance/declination forms
Employee health file (confidential)
TB training records

policies.title: Grievances, Complaints and Ombudsman Access
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Home (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Home (10A NCAC 13G): all residents, family members, responsible persons and staff
policies.purpose: To give residents and families a simple way to raise a concern or complaint. To make sure the facility responds, resolves the matter and documents it. To make sure residents know the outside agencies they can contact at any time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] welcomes grievances. Residents have the right to dignity and privacy, to be free of abuse, neglect and exploitation, and to private communication, and they may raise concerns without fear (G.S. 131D-21). The facility will not retaliate against any resident, family member or employee who files a grievance or contacts an outside agency. The Long-Term Care Ombudsman has access to residents. This policy meets 10A NCAC 13G .0704 (and 13F .1211(9) and .0704), as follows. Item 8a (Procedure for residents or family member to file a grievance) is met by Procedures 1-4. Item 8b (Procedure for follow-up of resident/family grievances by facility) is met by Procedures 5-9. Item 8c (Procedure for documentation of grievances and follow-up) is met by Procedures 10-12. Item 8d (Contact information for outside resources if grievances are not resolved) is met by Procedure 13 and the list in this policy.

definitions.definition: Any complaint or concern raised by or for a resident about care, services, staff, other residents, charges, the environment, rights, or any facility decision, whether spoken or written.
The Administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], or a person the Administrator designates in writing, who receives and resolves grievances.
The person who advocates for residents of long-term care facilities in the facility's region, at no cost to the resident. [REGIONAL OMBUDSMAN NAME], [PHONE].
Any action taken against a person because of a grievance, such as threats, changed care, withheld services, harassment, increased charges or discharge.

procedures: At admission, staff explain this policy to the resident and responsible person, give them a written copy and review it with the resident rights in RR-01. The copy gives the Grievance Officer's name and phone, and the outside contacts listed in Procedure 13. The resident's acknowledgment is kept in the record.

A resident, family member or responsible person may file a grievance verbally or in writing, by any of these methods: telling any staff member, telling the Administrator in person or by phone at [PHONE], writing a note, using the Grievance Form available at [LOCATION], or dropping a note in the grievance box at [LOCATION] that the Administrator opens each business day. A grievance may be made anonymously.

Any staff member who hears a grievance writes it down on a Grievance Form the same day, and gives it to the Administrator by the next business day. If the grievance involves abuse, neglect or exploitation, the staff member tells the Administrator immediately and the facility follows INC-03. Staff may not discourage, ignore or delay a grievance.

Staff help residents who cannot write or who need language, hearing, vision or cognitive assistance (see RR-05) to file a grievance. A resident may ask a family member, friend or the Ombudsman to help or speak for them.
The Grievance Officer acknowledges each grievance to the resident or person who filed it within 1 business day, in person or by phone, and records the date.

The Grievance Officer investigates promptly. This includes talking with the resident and any involved staff, reviewing records and observing the situation. A grievance that suggests risk to a resident's health or safety is handled immediately.
The Grievance Officer works with the resident or complainant on a resolution. Where it affects care, the Officer updates the resident's care plan (ADM-03) and informs the physician if needed.

The Grievance Officer gives the complainant a response within 7 calendar days. The response is written when the complainant asks or the matter is serious. The response states the findings, the action taken or planned, and the date it will be done. If more time is needed, the Officer tells the complainant why and gives a new date.

The Officer follows up with the complainant after the resolution. This is usually within 14 days. The Officer asks if the resident is satisfied and records the answer. If not satisfied, the Officer tells the complainant about the outside resources in Procedure 13.

The Grievance Officer records every grievance on the Grievance Log. The log shows date received, resident, person who filed, nature of the concern, staff involved, investigation steps, resolution, date of response, date of follow-up and the resident's satisfaction.

Each completed Grievance Form is kept with the log. Investigative notes are kept with it. The matter is also noted in the resident record only where it affects care. Grievance records are kept [NUMBER] years and are available to surveyors.

The Administrator reviews the Grievance Log at least quarterly for trends, takes corrective action and reports the findings to the Quality Assurance review under GOV-04. Staff are retrained when patterns are found.

Outside resources are posted in a place residents can see, given to each resident at admission, and included in any written grievance response. Residents may contact them at any time, privately and without staff permission. The facility lists: (a) Regional Long-Term Care Ombudsman: [NAME], [PHONE]; (b) County Department of Social Services (Adult Home Specialist): [NAME], [PHONE]; (c) NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation, Adult Care Licensure Section: 919-855-3765, DHSR.AdultCare.Questions@dhhs.nc.gov. The Administrator checks that these names and numbers are current at least every 6 months and whenever a change is reported.

The Ombudsman has access to residents. The facility lets the Ombudsman and representatives of ACLS and county DSS visit and speak privately with residents, and allows them to review records with resident consent or as the law allows.
Residents may use a phone privately to call these agencies or anyone else (G.S. 131D-21). A phone is available at [LOCATION] and staff help residents place calls on request.

The facility does not retaliate. Staff who threaten, punish or treat a resident or complainant differently because of a grievance are subject to discipline, up to dismissal (see STF-04). Anyone who believes retaliation has occurred may report it to the Administrator or to the outside agencies in Procedure 13.

If the grievance concerns a notice of discharge or transfer, the facility explains the resident's right to appeal and gives the contacts in the Notice of Discharge, which include the Ombudsman and the discharge team contact (10A NCAC 13F .0702; see ADM-05).

responsibilities.duty: Receives, investigates and resolves grievances, maintains the log, reviews trends and ensures no retaliation.
Accept and record grievances, report them to the Administrator within 1 business day, help residents file, and never retaliate.
Responds to urgent concerns on the spot and notifies the Administrator immediately of any safety-related grievance.

documentation: Grievance Forms
Grievance Log
Written responses and follow-up notes
Resident acknowledgment of grievance policy
Posted outside agency contact list and dates of review
Quarterly grievance trend review for QA

policies.title: Refunds, Deposits and Prepaid Fees
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Home (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Home (10A NCAC 13G): all private-pay and Special Assistance residents and responsible persons
policies.purpose: To explain clearly how deposits and prepaid fees are refunded when a resident leaves, dies or is discharged. To make sure refund terms are in writing in the resident contract. To protect Special Assistance residents from charges above the state maximum.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] states its refund rules in writing in the resident contract (CON-01) and gives the resident a written statement of services and charges at admission (G.S. 131D-21). This policy meets 10A NCAC 13G .1104/.1105 item 9 (Refund Policy) (and 10A NCAC 13F .1104/.1105) as follows. The facility refunds unused prepaid amounts, and any deposit that is owed, to the resident or the resident's estate. Refund amounts and timing are shown in the contract and are processed as stated in Procedures 5-12. For a facility-initiated discharge, the facility gives 30 days' written notice unless the discharge is urgent under 10A NCC 13F .0702. For a resident-initiated discharge, the administrator may require up to 14 days' written notice only if the resident contract says so. Special Assistance residents are never charged above the maximum rate set by the State.

definitions.definition: Money paid before or at admission to hold a bed or cover possible costs. It is refundable as the contract states.
Room, board and service charges paid in advance for a period that has not yet passed.
The monthly rate divided by the number of days in that month, used to calculate charges and refunds for partial months.
State/County Special Assistance room-and-board payments for eligible residents of adult care homes and family care homes. Payment is at the rate set by NC DHHS Division of Social Services.
The person who signed the contract for the resident and who receives refunds and notices on the resident's behalf.

procedures: Before admission, the Administrator reviews the contract's fee and refund sections with the resident and responsible person and answers questions. The resident signs and receives a copy. The contract states: amount of any deposit; what it covers; when and how refunds are made; the notice required; and how the final charge is figured.
The facility collects only fees listed in the written contract and statement of services and charges. It does not collect any other fee, and does not charge for services it is required to provide.

Any deposit or prepaid amount is recorded in a receipt given to the payer on the same day it is received. The receipt shows date, amount, purpose and the name of the staff member who received it. Money is deposited into the facility account by the next business day and is tracked in the resident's account ledger.

The facility's refund terms for a bed-hold or admission deposit are stated in the contract. The deposit is returned if the facility cannot admit the resident, if the resident does not move in because of a change in health or death before admission, or as the contract states.

Facility-initiated discharge: The facility may discharge only for the reasons allowed in 10A NCAC 13F .0702 and gives 30 days' written notice unless the discharge is urgent (see ADM-05). The resident is charged only for days up to the discharge date. The facility refunds any prepaid amount for days after the resident leaves.

Resident-initiated discharge: The resident or responsible person gives written notice. The contract may require up to 14 days' written notice, and only if the contract says so. The facility does not require notice where waiting would jeopardize the resident's health or safety, such as an emergency hospital admission or a move to a higher level of care ordered by a physician. The Administrator also documents contacts with possible discharge locations as required (see ADM-05).

On the day the resident leaves, the Administrator or business office prepares a Final Account Statement. It shows charges to the last day of stay under the contract, any notice period charge allowed by the contract, any deposit, payments received and any resident funds held (see RR-02).

The facility refunds any amount owed to the resident or responsible person within [NUMBER] days after the resident leaves, as stated in the contract. Refunds are paid by check or electronic transfer, and the payer signs a receipt.

Death: Charges stop at the end of the day the resident dies, or on the date the resident's belongings are removed if the contract says so and the contract treats this as part of the stay. The facility refunds prepaid amounts and deposits to the resident's estate or legal representative within the time stated in the contract. Resident funds and property are handled under RR-02 and HLT-08.
Hospital stay or temporary absence: The contract states whether charges continue while the resident is away and whether the bed is held. The facility does not charge for a bed it has re-assigned.

Special Assistance residents: The facility charges no more than the SA rate set by NC DHHS Division of Social Services for room and board and does not ask the resident or family for extra payments for services covered by that rate. The resident's personal needs allowance belongs to the resident (see RR-02). The facility returns any overpayment received from or for an SA resident promptly and notifies the county DSS when the SA rate or the resident's status changes (see GOV-05).

Disputes: If a resident or responsible person disagrees with a refund calculation, the Administrator reviews the account within 5 business days and gives a written explanation. The matter may also be raised as a grievance (GRV-01), and the resident may contact the Ombudsman or the county DSS.
Refund records and Final Account Statements are filed in the resident's financial record, kept under REC-01, and available to the surveyor on request.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure the contract states refund and notice terms, approves refunds, and ensures SA charges stay within the state maximum.
Issues receipts, maintains ledgers, prepares Final Account Statements and issues refunds on time.
Gives written notice as the contract requires and provides a forwarding address for refunds.

documentation: Signed resident contract and statement of services and charges
Deposit and payment receipts
Resident account ledger
Written discharge or move-out notice
Final Account Statement
Refund check or transfer record and signed receipt
SA rate and county DSS correspondence

policies.category: Visitation in Facility & Sign Out Log
policies.title: Visitation and Resident Sign-Out Log
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Home (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Home (10A NCAC 13G): all residents, visitors and staff
policies.purpose: To protect each resident's right to see visitors and communicate privately, and to keep the home safe and orderly. To track each resident's whereabouts using a sign-out/sign-in log.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] welcomes visitors and supports each resident's right to private communication and phone access (G.S. 131D-21). The facility keeps a visitor policy and a resident sign-out/sign-in log.
