The Administrator gives the resident a plain-language explanation of what we do with directives: file them, share them with treating providers, and honor them. The explanation is given in a language and format the resident understands (see RR-05).

If the resident has a directive, the Administrator or designee obtains a copy at admission. If it is not available that day, staff request it and record the follow-up date; the Administrator checks that it is received within 14 days.

The staff member receiving the copy checks that it is signed and dated, writes on the record where the original is kept (for example, with the resident, a family member or an attorney), and does not alter or interpret the document.

If the resident has no directive, the Administrator tells the resident that one is optional, that it can be completed later with the resident's physician or attorney, and that [AGENCY NAME] will honor it once it is provided. Staff do not pressure residents to sign one and do not advise on its content.
Copies are filed in the 'Advance Directives' section at the front of the resident record. The face sheet is marked 'Directive on file' with the type of document and the date.

If the resident has a DNR order or MOST form, the Administrator makes sure the original or a clearly marked copy is kept where staff can get it immediately in an emergency: [LOCATION OF EMERGENCY INFORMATION] and in the transfer packet. The location is posted in the staff-only area.

At orientation (STF-03), each new employee is told where advance directives are filed and where DNR/MOST forms are kept. The Administrator reminds staff at least annually and whenever the filing location changes.

In an emergency, staff call 911 and the Administrator or manager, then follow the resident's DNR/MOST order as written and as EMS directs. If staff are unsure whether a form is valid, they call 911, follow dispatcher instructions, and hand the actual form to EMS. Staff who are not authorized to interpret medical orders do not make that decision alone.

When a resident is transferred to a hospital or other provider (see HLT-03), the staff member preparing the transfer packet includes copies of all directives and DNR/MOST forms and tells the receiving staff, by phone or in writing, that they are enclosed. The transfer is documented in the record.

When hospice or home health is involved (see HLT-07), the Administrator gives the agency copies of directives at the first visit and confirms in writing that hospice's orders and the directives are consistent. Differences are referred to the physician and the resident's representative.

At each annual assessment, care plan review (ADM-02, ADM-03) and change of condition, the care plan coordinator asks if the resident's wishes or documents have changed. Updated documents replace outdated ones in the active section; superseded copies are marked 'Superseded' with the date and kept in the record.

A resident with capacity may change or revoke a directive at any time. The staff member who hears the request reports it to the Administrator the same day. The Administrator documents it, notifies the physician, and updates the face sheet and emergency location.

If family members or staff disagree with a documented wish, the Administrator contacts the resident (or representative) and the physician, records the discussion, and continues to honor the directive unless the resident or authorized representative changes it.
At the time of death, staff follow HLT-08 and give the funeral home or medical examiner any required documents as directed.
The Administrator reviews advance directive filing, face sheet flags and emergency access for a sample of records each quarter and reports results through the QA program (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures advance directive inquiry occurs at admission and reassessment, directives are filed, DNR/MOST forms are accessible, and staff are trained; handles disagreements and revocations.
Collects and files directives, updates the face sheet, prepares transfer packets and keeps the emergency location current.

responsibilities.role: Direct care staff and medication aides
responsibilities.duty: Know where directives are kept, call 911 in emergencies, give forms to EMS, and report a resident's changed wishes to the Administrator.
Provides copies, tells the home when wishes change, and tells the physician of any changes.

documentation: Admission checklist showing the advance directive inquiry, date and response
Copies of directives, DNR orders and MOST forms in the 'Advance Directives' section of the record
Record face sheet flag and note of the original's location
Transfer packet checklist and notes on communication with EMS, hospital and hospice
Notes of annual and change-of-condition reviews and any revocation
Staff orientation and annual training records
Quarterly QA audit results

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Homes (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Homes (10A NCAC 13G) — all staff, volunteers, contractors and students
policies.purpose: To protect each resident's right to dignity, privacy, private communication and confidential records under N.C.G.S. §131D-21, and to meet HIPAA privacy requirements (45 CFR Part 160 and 45 CFR 164.530) where they apply to [AGENCY NAME].
policies.policy: Residents have the right to privacy and confidential records under N.C.G.S. §131D-21. [AGENCY NAME] gives each resident a privacy notice at admission, limits staff access to the minimum information needed for their job, and releases resident information only with written authorization or as the law allows, for example to the NC Division of Health Service Regulation (DHSR) Adult Care Licensure Section, the county Department of Social Services (DSS) and the long-term care ombudsman. To the extent [AGENCY NAME] is a HIPAA covered entity (for example, because it bills Medicaid electronically), it follows 45 CFR Part 160 and the administrative requirements of 45 CFR 164.530, including a designated privacy official, workforce training, safeguards, a complaint process, sanctions and no retaliation. We apply the same standards to all residents as a matter of policy, whether or not HIPAA covers a particular activity. Residents also have the right to private communication and to phone access (N.C.G.S. §131D-21).

definitions.definition: Individually identifiable information about a resident's health, care or payment, in any form: paper, electronic or spoken.
Using, sharing or asking for only as much PHI as needed to do a task, such as giving care, billing or complying with law.
A signed, dated written permission from the resident or representative to share specific information with a specific person or organization for a stated purpose.
The person designated by [AGENCY NAME] to develop and carry out privacy procedures and receive privacy complaints.

procedures: The Administrator designates a privacy official ([PRIVACY OFFICIAL NAME]) in writing. If no one else is named, the Administrator holds this role. The designation is filed in the administrative binder.

At admission, the Administrator or designee gives the resident or representative the written privacy notice, explains it, and obtains a signed acknowledgment filed in the record. If the resident refuses to sign, staff note the refusal and date.

At orientation (STF-03) and at least annually, every employee, volunteer and contractor with access to residents or records is trained on this policy and signs a confidentiality statement. Training dates are kept in the personnel record.

Access to resident records follows job duty. Direct care staff see the records of residents they serve; the Administrator and manager see all records; billing staff see only what billing needs. The Administrator reviews who has access at least once a year.

Paper records are kept in a locked cabinet or room, are never left open on counters or carts, and are returned after use. Electronic records require unique passwords, automatic screen locks and no password sharing. Staff do not text or email resident information on unsecured personal accounts.

Staff discuss resident information only where others cannot overhear. Shift reports, care discussions and phone calls about residents are not held in dining rooms, hallways or common areas where visitors or other residents can hear.

Staff knock and wait for permission before entering a resident's room unless there is an emergency; they close doors and curtains during personal care and keep residents covered. Residents may have private conversations and private visits in a space that respects their dignity.

Residents have access to a telephone and may make and receive private calls, send and receive unopened mail, and use other private communication. Staff do not open, read or screen mail or listen to calls. Reasonable limits on hours are posted only if they do not restrict calls at reasonable times.

Before releasing information to anyone outside the care team, staff check for a valid signed authorization or a legal basis. Staff refer requests from family, attorneys, insurers and the media to the Administrator, who verifies identity and the authorization before anything is released.

Information may be released without authorization as the law allows, including to DHSR surveyors, county DSS, the ombudsman, adult protective services, law enforcement as required by law, and treating providers, EMS and hospitals in a transfer or emergency. The Administrator records what was released, to whom, when, and the basis for release.

Staff do not take photos, video or audio of residents, or post anything about residents on social media, without the resident's written consent filed in the record. Staff personal phones are not used to take resident photographs.

Residents or representatives who ask to see or copy a record are referred to the Administrator, who makes it available within a reasonable time and records the request. Requests to correct a record are reviewed by the Administrator and documented.

Staff who see or suspect an improper use or disclosure report it to the privacy official the same day. The privacy official investigates, takes steps to limit harm, decides with legal counsel whether any notice to the resident or others is required, and documents the outcome.

Residents and families may make a privacy complaint to the privacy official or through GRV-01. [AGENCY NAME] does not retaliate against anyone who makes a complaint in good faith. The complaint and response are documented.
Staff who violate this policy are subject to discipline up to and including termination, applied consistently and documented in the personnel record (see STF-04).
Privacy documentation required by 45 CFR 164.530 is kept according to REC-01 (HIPAA documentation for at least six years), and the Administrator reviews this policy at least annually under GOV-03.

responsibilities.duty: Designates the privacy official, ensures training and safeguards, approves releases of information and enforces sanctions.
Maintains privacy procedures, notice and acknowledgments, investigates complaints and incidents, and keeps documentation.
Use only the minimum necessary information, protect records, report breaches and refer outside requests to the Administrator.
Reviews the privacy notice, provides or revokes authorizations, and raises privacy concerns.

documentation: Written designation of privacy official
Signed privacy notice acknowledgments
Signed authorizations and revocations
Disclosure log for releases outside the care team
Staff confidentiality statements and training records
Photo/media consent forms
Privacy complaint and incident files with investigation notes and outcomes
Annual access review and policy review records

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Homes (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Homes (10A NCAC 13G) — all staff, in admission, care, services and employment-related contact with residents and the public
policies.purpose: To make sure no one is denied admission, services or dignity because of race, color, national origin or disability, and that residents who speak limited English or have communication needs can understand and take part in their care, consistent with N.C.G.S. §131D-21, Title VI (42 USC 2000d) and the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 USC 12101 et seq.).
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate in admission, care, services, room assignment, activities or discharge on the basis of race, color, national origin or disability. We provide interpreters or translated materials to residents with limited English proficiency at no cost to them. We provide reasonable accommodations for disabilities. We honor each resident's dignity and personal preferences in care planning (N.C.G.S. §131D-21; see ADM-03). Admission and retention decisions are based on whether the home is licensed to serve the person and can meet the person's assessed needs within licensed capacity (ADM-01, ADM-04), applied the same way to all applicants. A disability alone is never the reason to deny or end services; the decision is individualized and documented.

definitions.definition: A limited ability to speak, read, write or understand English well enough to take part in one's own care or in decisions.

A person competent in both languages and in the terms being used, who keeps information confidential. This may be a trained staff member, a contracted interpreter or a telephone/video interpreter service.

A change in a policy, practice, communication method or service that lets a person with a disability have an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the home's services, unless it would fundamentally change the services or cause an undue burden.
Tools or services that make communication effective for persons with hearing, vision or speech disabilities, such as large print, readers, amplified phones or sign language interpreters.

procedures: The Administrator posts a nondiscrimination statement in the public area near the license and resident rights (see GOV-02 and RR-01) and includes it in the admission packet. The statement says the home does not discriminate based on race, color, national origin or disability and tells how to complain.

At pre-admission and admission, staff ask each applicant and representative what language they prefer for spoken and written information and whether they have communication, vision, hearing, mobility or cognitive needs. The answers are recorded in the record and care plan.

Admission decisions follow the written criteria in ADM-01 and ADM-04. The Administrator documents the reason for any denial in terms of license, capacity or ability to meet assessed needs, and reviews the denial for consistency with this policy before it is communicated.

For a resident or representative with limited English, staff arrange a qualified interpreter or language line for the admission interview, contract review, rights explanation, assessment, care planning, consent discussions and medication or health teaching. The interpreter and time used are recorded.

Staff do not use other residents as interpreters. Family members interpret only if the resident asks for it, and staff note the request; a qualified interpreter is used for sensitive or medical topics unless the resident declines in writing after being offered one.

The Administrator provides, or obtains, translations of the resident contract, statement of services and charges, resident rights, privacy notice and grievance procedure in the languages most commonly used by residents. If a translation is not available, an interpreter reads the document aloud and staff document that this was done.

For residents with vision, hearing, speech or cognitive impairments, staff offer auxiliary aids such as large print, reading aloud, written notes, amplification, picture boards or extra time, and record the aids in the care plan.

A resident or representative may ask for a reasonable accommodation at any time, verbally or in writing, and any staff member who receives the request gives it to the Administrator the same day. The Administrator responds within 5 working days. If an accommodation is denied or an alternative offered, the Administrator explains why in writing and records it.

Staff make the building and activities usable by residents with disabilities, including reachable call devices, clear walkways and accessible dining and activity locations, and report barriers to the Administrator for correction (see DLV-01).

Care plans (ADM-03) record each resident's preferences for daily routine, meals, dress, privacy, culture, language and religion, and staff honor these preferences consistent with safety and the resident's rights.

Staff treat residents with courtesy and do not use slurs, stereotypes, demeaning language or differences in service based on a protected characteristic. Observed or reported discrimination is reported to the Administrator and handled under GRV-01 and STF-04.

Any resident, family member or employee may complain of discrimination to the Administrator or through GRV-01, or to the ombudsman. The Administrator investigates, responds in writing and does not allow retaliation. If the complaint involves the Administrator, it goes to [GOVERNING BODY CONTACT].

At orientation (STF-03) and at least annually, staff are trained on this policy, how to reach interpreters, how to offer auxiliary aids and how to refer accommodation requests. Training records are kept in personnel files.
The Administrator keeps a current list of interpreter and language line contacts ([INTERPRETER SERVICE NAME], [PHONE]) in the staff area and at the front desk.
Each quarter the Administrator reviews denials, accommodation requests, interpreter use and complaints for patterns and reports the findings through QA (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Applies admission criteria consistently, arranges interpreters and translations, decides on accommodation requests, investigates complaints and ensures training.
Identifies language and communication needs at admission, records aids in care plans and keeps interpreter contacts available.
Treat residents with dignity, use interpreters and aids as arranged, and report requests, barriers and discrimination.
Reviews the quarterly report and addresses discrimination complaints involving the Administrator.

documentation: Posted and distributed nondiscrimination statement
Language and communication needs recorded at admission and in care plan
Interpreter and language line use log
Translated documents or record of interpreted reading
Accommodation request forms and written responses
Documented reasons for any admission denial
Discrimination complaint files
Training records and quarterly QA summary

policies.title: Pre-Admission Screening and Admission Criteria
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Homes (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Homes (10A NCAC 13G) — Administrator, managers and staff involved in admissions
policies.purpose: To admit only residents whom the home is licensed to serve and can care for safely within licensed capacity, to apply criteria the same way to every applicant, and to state the admission and discharge policies required for licensure.
policies.policy: This policy, together with ADM-04 (Retention Limits and Conditions the Facility Cannot Serve) and ADM-05 (Discharge, Transfer and Relocation Notice; Discharge Appeals), meets Family Care Home licensing checklist item FCH-2.b(iii) — 'The admission and discharge policies' (License a Family Care Home, Procedures step 2.b). It applies to Adult Care Homes as well. [AGENCY NAME] admits a person only when the home can meet the person's needs within licensed capacity. The number of residents never exceeds the number on the license (10A NCAC 13F .0206 for ACHs; 10A NCAC 13G .0206 for FCHs). An ACH's bed capacity and services must also comply with its Certificate of Need (CON). In an FCH, capacity is 2–6 residents and depends on the building code and each resident's evacuation capability; the license lists ambulatory and non-ambulatory capacity, and we admit no resident whose evacuation capability would exceed those limits. Each resident signs a contract at admission (CON-01), receives a medical examination, TB test and immunizations as required by the Adult Care Home rules (see INF-05), and is assessed within 30 days of admission (10A NCAC 13F .0801; ADM-02). Discharge is covered in ADM-04 and ADM-05: a resident is discharged only for the reasons and with the notice described there. Before offering any respite stay, the Administrator checks whether the Medical Care Commission has amended the respite care rules under N.C.G.S. §131D-6.1 (effective July 1, 2026) and follows the current rules.

definitions.definition: The maximum number of residents shown on the home's license (7 or more for an ACH; 2–6 for an FCH). For an FCH the license lists ambulatory and non-ambulatory capacity.
Whether a resident can evacuate the building without help (ambulatory) or needs help or cannot evacuate on their own (non-ambulatory), as determined for licensing and life safety.
The review of an applicant's needs, health information, behaviors and preferences before admission to decide whether the home can serve the applicant.
A short-term stay arranged for a person who is not a long-term resident, offered only if current State rules permit.
Certificate of Need, which is required for new adult care home beds; bed capacity and services in an ACH must comply with the CON.

procedures: The Administrator receives each inquiry and records it on the inquiry log. Staff give the applicant or representative a copy of the admission criteria and the services and charges, and do not make admission promises before screening.

Before any admission, the Administrator or a designee who meets the qualifications in Rule .0508 completes a pre-admission screening using the applicant's health information, physician or hospital records, current medications, diagnoses, ADLs, behaviors, mobility and evacuation ability, and the applicant's own wishes. The screening is dated and signed.

The Administrator checks that the home is licensed to serve the applicant and that the applicant does not have a condition the home cannot serve (ADM-04). The checked criteria are written on the screening form.

The Administrator confirms current census against the number on the license. If admission would exceed licensed capacity, the applicant is placed on a waiting list or referred elsewhere and no admission occurs. For an ACH, the Administrator also confirms that the bed and services are within the CON.

For an FCH, the Administrator confirms that the applicant's evacuation capability fits the licensed ambulatory/non-ambulatory capacity. If it would not, the applicant is not admitted. If admitting or keeping a resident would change the home's evacuation capability, or a non-resident will live in the home, the Administrator notifies the Adult Care Licensure Section (ACLS) at 919-855-3765 before the change takes place. If a resident becomes temporarily non-ambulatory, the Administrator immediately notifies the DHSR Construction Section at 919-855-3893 and documents the call.

Applicants are reviewed on the same criteria regardless of race, color, national origin or disability (RR-05). The Administrator documents a reason tied to licensure, capacity or ability to meet assessed needs for any denial and tells the applicant, in writing, on request.

The Administrator checks that the applicant has the medical examination, TB test (see INF-05) and immunization information required by the Adult Care Home rules, and that these are signed and dated by the proper provider before or at admission. Missing items are obtained by the time set in the rules and tracked on the admission checklist.

Before admission, the applicant or representative receives the written statement of services and charges, the resident contract (CON-01), the Residents' Bill of Rights (RR-01), the privacy notice (RR-04), the grievance procedure (GRV-01) and the discharge and transfer provisions in ADM-05. The Administrator reviews the documents with the applicant, using an interpreter if needed.

The applicant or representative and the Administrator sign the contract at admission. The signed contract is filed in the record, and a copy is given to the resident or representative on the day of admission.

At admission the Administrator asks about advance directives (RR-03), identifies the resident's emergency contacts and physician, and records the resident's medications and any self-administration ability (MED-01, MED-02).
Staff prepare interim care instructions from the screening for the first days after admission, tell all shifts, and place the resident in a room appropriate to their needs and preferences.

The resident is assessed within 30 days of admission using the DHSR assessment instrument or an equivalent (10A NCAC 13F .0801; ADM-02), and the care plan is developed from it (ADM-03). The Administrator calendars the due date on the admission checklist.

Before offering respite care, the Administrator checks the Division of Health Service Regulation website or calls ACLS at 919-855-3765 to learn whether the respite rules under N.C.G.S. §131D-6.1 have been amended, and follows the current rules on screening, length of stay, paperwork and capacity. The check and date are recorded. If the rules cannot be confirmed, no respite stay is offered.
Admissions are accepted only on days and times when enough staff are on duty to meet the new resident's needs (STF-01). The Administrator records that staffing was checked.
If a resident's needs later exceed what the home can serve, the Administrator follows ADM-04 and ADM-05 for retention, discharge and notice.
The Administrator reviews admission and denial records and licensed capacity use each quarter and reports through QA (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Decides on admission, confirms capacity, CON compliance and evacuation capability, signs contracts, makes required notices to ACLS and the Construction Section, and checks respite rules.
Completes the pre-admission screening and admission checklist and records findings accurately.
Prepares interim care instructions, tracks medical exam, TB and assessment due dates and orients the resident.
Approves admission criteria and capacity decisions.

documentation: Inquiry log and waiting list
Dated pre-admission screening form and documentation of any denial reason
Admission checklist: capacity check, CON check (ACH), evacuation capability (FCH), medical exam, TB test, immunizations
Signed resident contract and written statement of services and charges
Notices to ACLS or the Construction Section and call notes
Respite rules check record
Assessment due-date tracking and quarterly QA review

policies.title: Resident Assessment and Reassessment
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Homes (10A NCAC 13F .0801) and Family Care Homes (10A NCAC 13G .0801) — Administrator, assessors and care staff
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident receives a complete functional assessment within 30 days of admission, annually, and after any significant change of condition, so that care is based on the resident's actual needs.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] assesses each resident within 30 days of admission and annually, as required by 10A NCC 13F .0801 for ACHs and 10A NCAC 13G .0801 for FCHs. We also reassess after a significant change of condition. We use the DHSR assessment instrument or an equivalent. The assessor must meet Rule .0508, and if the home uses its own instrument, the assessor must also have training on it. The assessment is functional and covers psychosocial status, cognition, and activities of daily living (ADLs), as well as diagnoses, medications, ability to self-administer medications, mental health history, social history, mood and behavior, nutrition, skin, and vision and hearing. The assessment is the basis for the resident's care plan (ADM-03).

definitions.definition: An evaluation of what the resident can and cannot do, and how much help is needed, in daily life, including psychosocial, cognitive and ADL status.
Basic self-care tasks such as bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, walking, eating and grooming.
The person designated by the Administrator who meets Rule .0508 and has completed training on the assessment instrument if it is the home's own instrument.

A change in a resident's physical, mental, behavioral or functional status that is more than temporary, is not expected to resolve without intervention, or affects the resident's care needs (examples: new decline in ADLs, hospitalization with lasting loss of function, new onset of confusion, major behavior change).
The resident assessment form published by the NC Division of Health Service Regulation for adult care homes and family care homes.

procedures: The Administrator names in writing one or more assessors who meet Rule .0508 and keeps proof of qualifications in the personnel file (STF-02). If the home uses its own instrument, the Administrator also records the assessor's training on it.

The Administrator decides whether the home will use the current DHSR instrument or an equivalent. If an equivalent is used, the Administrator compares it with the DHSR instrument to confirm that every required area is covered, and keeps the comparison on file.
At admission, the Administrator enters the 30-day assessment due date on the admission checklist and the facility calendar. The assessment is completed on or before that day.

The assessor completes the assessment by direct contact with the resident, observation of the resident doing daily tasks, interviews with the resident, representative and staff, and review of physician orders, diagnoses and medication lists. The assessor does not complete it from records alone.

The assessment covers at least: diagnoses; medications; the resident's ability to self-administer medications; ADLs; mental health history; social history; mood and behavior; nutrition; skin condition; cognition; and vision and hearing, along with psychosocial status.

The assessor uses the resident's language and communication method, with an interpreter or aids as needed (RR-05), and asks about the resident's preferences, which are written on the assessment for the care plan.

The assessor signs and dates the assessment with credentials and gives it to the Administrator for review within 2 working days. The Administrator checks that it is complete and consistent with the pre-admission screening (ADM-01).

Findings that suggest a need for services the home cannot provide (ADM-04), a physician evaluation or a referral (for example, new confusion, weight loss, skin breakdown or fall risk) are reported to the Administrator the same day and to the resident's physician as required by HLT-03.
The care plan is developed or updated from the assessment (ADM-03). The assessment and care plan are filed in the resident record (REC-01).
The annual reassessment is due within 12 months of the last assessment. The Administrator's calendar flags it 30 days before the due date, and the assessor completes it by the due date.

A reassessment is also completed after a significant change of condition. Any staff member who notices a change reports it to the Administrator or manager the same day. The Administrator decides within 2 working days whether the change is significant, records the decision, and has the reassessment completed promptly.

After a hospital stay, rehabilitation stay or return from a transfer (HLT-03), the manager reviews discharge papers and orders, and the Administrator decides whether a reassessment is needed. The decision and reason are documented.

The resident and the representative are told about the findings of each assessment in plain language and may ask questions or request changes. Their comments and any disagreements are written on or attached to the assessment.
Assessments are kept where the Administrator, assessors and authorized staff can get them, and under the confidentiality rules in RR-04.
The Administrator checks, at least quarterly, that all assessments are on time and complete and reports overdue or incomplete assessments through QA (GOV-04), with a plan to correct them.

responsibilities.duty: Designates qualified assessors, selects the instrument, ensures timelines, reviews each assessment and decides when a significant change requires reassessment.
Completes the assessment in person using the instrument, records findings and resident preferences, and promptly reports concerns.
Give accurate information about the resident and report changes of condition promptly.
Take part in the assessment and share preferences and concerns.

documentation: Completed, signed and dated assessments (admission, annual, change of condition)
Written designation of assessors and proof of Rule .0508 qualifications and instrument training
Comparison with the DHSR instrument if an equivalent is used
Assessment due-date calendar and tracking log
Record of significant-change decisions and referrals
Quarterly QA review of assessment timeliness

policies.title: Resident Care Plan
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Homes (10A NCAC 13F .0802) and Family Care Homes (10A NCAC 13G) — Administrator, assessors, managers and all direct care staff
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident has a written, resident-centered care plan based on the assessment, that staff can find and follow it, and that it is kept current.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] develops and implements a resident-centered care plan for every resident, based on the assessment required by 10A NCAC 13F .0801 (ADM-02) and including the resident's care preferences, as required by 10A NCAC 13F .0802. We keep a copy of the current plan where staff can access it. We update the plan after each reassessment and whenever the resident's condition changes. The care plan guides daily care, supervision, medication assistance, meals, activities and referrals, and every staff member who cares for the resident must know and follow it.

definitions.definition: A written plan that states the resident's assessed needs, the care and services to be provided, who provides them, how often, and the resident's preferences.
Built around the resident's own goals, routines, culture, values and choices, developed with the resident and the representative, not only around what is convenient for the home.
The most recently reviewed and updated version, which reflects the latest assessment and any changes in condition or orders.

procedures: The Administrator assigns a care plan coordinator for each resident, who may be the assessor, and records the assignment on the admission checklist.
At admission, staff prepare short interim care instructions from the pre-admission screening (ADM-01) and share them with every shift until the full plan is complete.

After the assessment (ADM-02) is completed, the coordinator drafts the care plan from the assessment findings. The plan is completed no later than the assessment due date and in any event within 30 days of admission.

The coordinator meets with the resident, and with the representative if the resident wants, to discuss the findings and ask about preferences: wake and sleep times, bathing, dress, meals, activities, privacy, culture, religion, visitors and how the resident wants help given. These preferences are written into the plan in the resident's words as far as possible.

The plan addresses each need found in the assessment, including ADL help, supervision level, mobility and fall risk (HLT-05), skin (HLT-06), nutrition and diet (NUT-01), medication assistance (MED-01, MED-02), mood and behavior, cognition (HLT-04), wandering risk (WAN-01), activities (ACT-01), and vision and hearing.

For each need the plan states the goal, the interventions, who is responsible, how often and what to report. Services from hospice, home health or other outside providers are included and coordinated (HLT-07).

The plan uses non-restraint approaches to behavior and does not include physical restraints unless permitted under RST-01. Interventions that restrict a resident's rights are not included without legal authority and documentation.

The Administrator reviews, signs and dates the plan and checks it against the assessment and the resident's physician orders. The resident or representative is given the chance to review and sign, and any disagreement is recorded.

A copy of the current care plan is kept in the resident's record and in [CARE PLAN ACCESS LOCATION], where all staff who care for the resident can get it on every shift. It is kept private from visitors and other residents (RR-04).
Before working with a resident, each new staff member reads the resident's care plan and signs a log. The manager reviews important changes with staff at shift handoff and records the review.
Aides record the care they give so that the manager can compare daily care with the plan. Differences are reported to the manager the same day.

The coordinator updates the plan after every reassessment, annually, after a significant change of condition, after a hospitalization or return from transfer (HLT-03), when physician orders change and when the resident asks for a change. An update is made within 5 working days of the triggering event, or sooner if safety requires.
Replaced plans are marked 'Superseded' with the date and kept in the record. Only the current plan is kept at the staff access location so that no outdated plan is used.
If the resident refuses a care or service, staff respect the choice, explain risks, inform the Administrator, record the refusal and update the plan, notifying the physician where needed.
The Administrator checks care plans each quarter for completeness, resident preferences, staff access, and timely updates, and reports the results through QA (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Assigns coordinators, reviews and signs plans, makes sure current plans are accessible and ensures updates are timely.
Develops the plan from the assessment with the resident, records preferences, and updates it after changes.
Read and follow the current plan, document care given and report changes or refusals.
Share preferences, review the plan and ask for changes.

documentation: Signed and dated care plan with the resident's preferences
Interim care instructions
Record of review with the resident or representative and any disagreements
Staff read-and-sign log
Superseded plans kept in the record
Care plan update notes tied to each reassessment or change of condition
Quarterly QA review

policies.title: Retention Limits and Conditions the Facility Cannot Serve
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Home (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Home (10A NCAC 13G)
policies.purpose: To define when [AGENCY NAME] may continue to care for a resident and when a resident's needs or condition exceed what the facility is licensed, staffed and equipped to provide. This policy makes sure that a facility-initiated discharge is used only for a reason the rules allow, and only after the facility has tried to meet the resident's needs.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] retains a resident for as long as the facility can safely meet the resident's needs within its license, capacity, staffing and building. The facility starts a discharge only for a reason listed in 10A NCAC 13F .0702 and G.S. 131D-21(17): (1) the resident's needs cannot be met in the facility; (2) the resident's health has improved so that the resident no longer needs care in the facility; (3) the safety of other individuals in the facility is endangered, or the resident's own health or safety is endangered; (4) nonpayment of the bill after a written warning; or (5) a legal mandate (for example, closure or loss of license). The facility does not discharge or threaten to discharge a resident for any other reason, and never in retaliation for a complaint or the exercise of a resident right (see GRV-01 and RR-01). Before starting a discharge for unmet needs, the Administrator must document the efforts made to meet those needs, including added facility services, home health, hospice and physician-ordered services, and must consult the resident's physician and the responsible person. In a Family Care Home, the facility must keep within the capacity on its license, which is based on the building code and each resident's evacuation capability. It must notify ACLS if a resident's evacuation capability changes. All discharges follow ADM-05.

definitions.definition: Continued residence of a person in the facility after admission, based on the facility's ability to meet the person's needs safely.
A discharge the facility starts, as opposed to one the resident or the resident's legal representative starts.
The family member, friend or other person designated in the record to be contacted about the resident, as defined in 10A NCAC 13F .0102.
A resident's ability to leave the building in an emergency (ambulatory or non-ambulatory). In an FCH it determines the capacity listed on the license.
The resident requires care, supervision or services that the facility cannot lawfully or safely provide even after reasonable efforts, such as added services, home health and hospice.

procedures: The Administrator reviews each resident's status at every reassessment (ADM-02), at every care plan review (ADM-03), and any time HLT-03 identifies a significant change in condition. The review asks whether the facility can still meet the resident's needs.

Staff who notice a decline or a new need (increased assistance, new behaviors, wandering, falls, skin problems, new treatments) report it to the Administrator or manager the same shift and record it in the resident's record.

The Administrator compares the resident's current needs with the facility's license, staffing, building and services. For an FCH, the Administrator also compares them with the evacuation capability listed on the license.

Before any discharge is considered for unmet needs, the Administrator and care staff try to meet the needs. This may include changing the care plan, adding staff supervision, arranging physician-ordered home health or therapy, arranging hospice (HLT-07), or using the facility nurse (HLT-02). Each effort is dated and recorded in the resident's record.

The Administrator consults the resident's physician (or other prescriber) about the resident's condition and needs. The Administrator also contacts the resident and the responsible person to discuss the concerns and the options. The dates, names and outcomes of these contacts are documented.

In an FCH, if a resident's evacuation capability changes, the Administrator notifies ACLS. If a resident becomes temporarily non-ambulatory, the Administrator notifies the DHSR Construction Section immediately (919-855-3893). The Administrator documents the date and name of the person notified. The facility does not exceed the ambulatory and non-ambulatory capacity listed on its license.
In an FCH, the Administrator also notifies ACLS before a non-resident begins to live in the home.
If the needs can be met, the Administrator updates the care plan and continues the resident's stay. The Administrator records the decision and the reasons.

If the needs cannot be met after documented efforts, the Administrator confirms that the situation fits a discharge reason in 10A NCAC 13F .0702 and G.S. 131D-21(17), and writes down which reason applies and why.

For nonpayment, the Administrator first gives the resident and responsible person a written warning that states the amount due and the date by which payment must be made. A discharge for nonpayment may begin only after that warning period has passed without payment. The Administrator should also tell the resident about county Special Assistance eligibility (GOV-05).

Once a discharge reason is confirmed, the Administrator starts the notice and appeal procedure in ADM-05. This includes the written Notice of Discharge, the Hearing Request Form and contact information for the ombudsman and the local resident discharge team.

If the resident's health or safety, or another resident's, is in immediate danger, the Administrator may use the urgent discharge path in ADM-05. The Administrator calls 911 or arranges emergency transfer as needed (HLT-03) and documents the facts that support the urgency.
The Administrator reviews every facility-initiated discharge with the governing body at the next quality meeting (GOV-04) to see whether admission screening (ADM-01) or staffing needs to change.

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether needs can be met, documents efforts and consultations, confirms the discharge reason, notifies ACLS and the Construction Section when required, and starts the discharge process.
Reports changes in resident condition to the Administrator the same shift and helps carry out care plan changes.
Observe and report changes in a resident's needs, abilities or behavior.
Is consulted about the resident's condition and needs and about added services or hospice.
Reviews facility-initiated discharges and any changes needed to admission or staffing practices.

documentation: Record of changes in condition and efforts to meet the resident's needs (dated)
Record of consultations with the physician, resident and responsible person
Written statement of the discharge reason selected and why it applies
Written warning for nonpayment (when applicable)
ACLS and Construction Section notification records (FCH)
Copies of discharge notices (see ADM-05)

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Relocation Notice; Discharge Appeals
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Home (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Home (10A NCAC 13G)
policies.purpose: To set out how [AGENCY NAME] admits, discharges and transfers residents so that every resident gets the written notice, the appeal rights and the help with relocation that North Carolina law requires.
policies.policy: This policy, together with ADM-01 (Pre-Admission Screening and Admission Criteria), ADM-04 and CON-01, meets License a Family Care Home, Procedures step 2.b(iii) — The admission and discharge policies. [AGENCY NAME] discharges a resident against the resident's wishes only for a reason allowed by G.S. 131D-21(17) and 10A NCAC 13F .0702 (see ADM-04). For a facility-initiated discharge, the Administrator gives a written Notice of Discharge with a Hearing Request Form. The Notice is hand delivered to the resident on the day it is dated, and a copy goes to the responsible person. At least 30 days' notice is given, unless the resident's or other residents' health or safety is in jeopardy, in which case a shorter urgent notice may be given. The Notice includes the reason for discharge, the effective date, how to appeal, and contact information for the Long-Term Care Ombudsman and the local adult care home resident discharge team. The resident may appeal through the NC Medicaid Hearing Office (G.S. 131D-4.8). Unless the law provides otherwise, the resident may stay in the facility until the appeal is resolved. The same notice, 30-day period and appeal protections apply in a Family Care Home under G.S. 131D-21(17). When a resident decides to leave, the facility may require up to 14 days' written notice only if the resident contract says so, and never where a delay would jeopardize the resident's health or safety. The Administrator documents contacts with possible discharge locations for every discharge.

definitions.definition: The written notice the facility gives to a resident it is discharging. It states the reason, the effective date, appeal rights and contacts.
The form delivered with the Notice of Discharge that the resident or representative uses to ask the NC Medicaid Hearing Office for an appeal.
A discharge on less than 30 days' notice because the resident's or other residents' health or safety is in jeopardy.

definitions.term: Local adult care home resident discharge team
definitions.definition: The local team established under G.S. 131D-4.8(e) that helps with placing residents who are being discharged.
A discharge the resident or the resident's legal representative decides to carry out.
The family member, friend or other person designated in the resident's record to be contacted and to receive copies of notices, as defined in 10A NCAC 13F .0102.

procedures: Admission: the Administrator confirms each admission under ADM-01 and CON-01, and the resident contract states the discharge reasons, the notice periods and, if used, the 14-day resident notice requirement.

Before any facility-initiated discharge, the Administrator completes the steps in ADM-04 (documented efforts to meet needs, consultation with the physician and the responsible person) and records the specific reason from 10A NCAC 13F .0702 and G.S. 131D-21(17).

The Administrator prepares the written Notice of Discharge. It states the reason, the effective date, the resident's right to appeal, how to complete and return the Hearing Request Form, and the names and telephone numbers of the Long-Term Care Ombudsman and the local adult care home resident discharge team.

The Administrator dates the Notice and hand delivers it with the Hearing Request Form to the resident on that same day. The Administrator reads or explains it in a manner the resident can understand, using interpreter or accessibility services as needed (RR-05).
On the same day, the Administrator sends or gives a copy of the Notice to the responsible person and legal representative, if any, and documents the date, time and method of delivery.

The Administrator gives at least 30 days' notice before the discharge date. Only if the resident's or other residents' health or safety is in jeopardy may the Administrator use a shorter notice. The Administrator then records the facts that show the jeopardy and the physician's input, if available.

The Administrator contacts the local adult care home resident discharge team and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman when the Notice is delivered, and asks the county Department of Social Services for help with placement for Special Assistance recipients.

The Administrator, with the resident and responsible person, identifies possible discharge locations (another licensed facility, family home, home with services, etc.). The Administrator contacts each one and documents the date, the place, the person contacted and the result. This documentation is kept for every discharge.

If the resident or representative appeals through the NC Medicaid Hearing Office, the Administrator keeps the resident in the facility until the appeal is resolved, unless the law provides otherwise. The Administrator also provides the Hearing Office with records and attends the hearing as required. The Administrator does not take any steps to force the resident out during the appeal.

For a resident-initiated discharge, the Administrator may ask for up to 14 days' written notice only if the resident contract states this requirement. The Administrator does not enforce this requirement if delay would jeopardize the resident's health or safety. The Administrator still documents contacts with possible discharge locations.

Before the resident leaves, the Administrator and nurse or supervisor review with the resident and responsible person the medications, the current care needs, follow-up appointments and any services arranged. Medications and records are released only under MED-02 and RR-04. Personal property and funds are returned and a signed receipt is kept (RR-02).

For a transfer to a hospital or another facility, the facility sends the medication list, MAR, face sheet and advance directive (see HLT-03 and RR-03). A hospital transfer for emergency treatment is not a discharge unless the facility decides not to take the resident back for a reason in ADM-04.
The Administrator completes any refund and final accounting under REF-01 and the contract, and sets out any amounts owed or refunded in writing.

The Administrator completes the discharge note in the resident's record, including the destination, who accompanied the resident, who was notified and when. The Administrator also files all notices and the appeal materials in the record (REC-01).
The Administrator reports discharges and related events to ACLS or the county as required by REC-02, and reviews each facility-initiated discharge at the next quality meeting (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Decides on and signs the Notice of Discharge, delivers it on the date it is written, contacts the ombudsman, discharge team and prospective locations, handles appeals and completes discharge documentation.
Prepares the medication list and transfer packet and helps with the resident's transition.
Prepares the final accounting and refund under REF-01 and RR-02.
May appeal a facility-initiated discharge and gives written notice when the resident chooses to leave.
Reviews discharges and appeals for patterns and compliance.

documentation: Signed and dated Notice of Discharge and Hearing Request Form, with proof of same-day hand delivery
Record of copy to responsible person (date, method)
Record of ombudsman, discharge team and county DSS contacts
Log of contacts with possible discharge locations (date, place, person, result)
Appeal documents and Hearing Office correspondence
Resident's written notice (resident-initiated discharge) and contract provision
Transfer packet checklist, personal property and funds receipt, final accounting
Discharge note in the resident record

policies.title: Personal Care, Supervision and Resident Services
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Home (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Home (10A NCAC 13G)
policies.purpose: To describe the personal care, supervision, services and accommodations [AGENCY NAME] provides, and to make sure residents receive them in a manner that is consistent with each resident's care plan and free from abuse and neglect.
policies.policy: This policy meets License a Family Care Home, Procedures step 2.b(iv) — The services and accommodation requirements. [AGENCY NAME] provides personal care and supervision to every resident according to the resident's care plan (ADM-03) and assessed needs (ADM-02). Personal care means assistance with the activities of daily living and the supervision residents need, as defined in G.S. 131D-2.1. Services include help with bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting, eating, mobility and transfers, medication assistance or administration (MED-01), meals and snacks (NUT-01), housekeeping and laundry (DLV-01), activities (ACT-01), arranging transportation (DLV-02), and coordination of health care. Accommodations are a safe, clean, comfortable living environment, with furnishings, bedding, linens and personal space as described in the resident contract (CON-01). Only staff who are trained and, where required, authorized perform aide duties and supervision as these terms are defined in 10A NCAC 13F .0102. Care is provided with dignity and respect. The failure to provide needed services, willful or grossly negligent infliction of pain, injury or mental anguish, or unreasonable confinement is abuse or neglect as defined in G.S. 131D-2.1 and is handled under INC-03.

definitions.definition: Assistance with activities of daily living and supervision that a resident needs, as defined in G.S. 131D-2.1.
Duties of staff who provide personal care and supervision to residents, as defined in 10A NCAC 13F .0102.
Observation and oversight of residents, and of staff, to make sure that care and safety needs are met, as defined in 10A NCAC 13F .0102.
The person designated to run the day-to-day operation of the facility in the Administrator's absence (see STF-05).

Defined in G.S. 131D-2.1. Abuse includes willful or grossly negligent infliction of pain, injury or mental anguish, unreasonable confinement, or deprivation of needed services by the administrator or staff.
1st shift 7:01 a.m. to 3:00 p.m.; 2nd shift 3:01 p.m. to 11:00 p.m.; 3rd shift 11:01 p.m. to 7:00 a.m. (10A NCAC 13F .0102).

procedures: At admission and after each assessment, the Administrator or nurse (ADM-02, ADM-03) identifies each resident's personal care and supervision needs and writes them into the care plan.
Each shift, the Administrator or manager assigns aides to residents and tasks. The assignment sheet is kept for the shift and shows who is responsible for each resident.
Before each shift, the outgoing staff give a report on residents' needs, changes, incidents and appointments to the incoming staff. The report is recorded in the shift communication log.

Aides give personal care as written in the care plan. This includes help with bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting and incontinence care, eating and drinking, walking and transfers, with attention to privacy, dignity and the resident's preferences.
Aides do not perform tasks outside their training or authorization. Tasks that require a licensed nurse, or an individual authorized under HLT-02 or MED-01, are referred to that person.

Staff supervise residents at the level in the care plan, including more frequent checks for residents at risk of falls (HLT-05), wandering (WAN-01) or skin breakdown (HLT-06). Staffing levels follow STF-01.
Aides document personal care on the resident's daily record or flow sheet at the time the care is given, as specified in the care plan.
The facility serves three meals daily plus snacks and fluids as described in NUT-01, and helps residents who need assistance eating.

The facility provides each resident with a clean, safe room and bedding, towels and linens, with laundry, housekeeping and maintenance carried out under DLV-01. Residents may keep personal belongings and furnishings as described in the contract and RR-02.
The facility offers activities (ACT-01) and arranges transportation (DLV-02) for medical appointments and other necessary trips as described in the resident contract.
Staff report any change in a resident's condition to the Administrator or manager at once, and follow HLT-03. Staff report any suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately under INC-03.

The Administrator or manager observes care at least weekly and checks that care is being given as planned and that residents' dignity is respected. Findings are recorded and used for training and quality improvement (GOV-04).

The Administrator reviews the services and accommodation list in the resident contract and the Policy and Procedure Manual at least annually to make sure it matches what the facility actually provides (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure that the services and accommodations described to residents are provided and that staff are trained for their duties.
Assigns staff, supervises care each shift and reports changes in condition.
Provide personal care and supervision as written in the care plan, document the care and report changes and concerns.
Perform or delegate nursing tasks under HLT-02.

documentation: Care plan (ADM-03) and assessment (ADM-02)
Daily personal care records / flow sheets
Shift assignment sheet and shift communication log
Supervisory observation notes
Resident contract describing services and accommodations (CON-01)

policies.title: Nursing Services and Delegation
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Home (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Home (10A NCAC 13G)
policies.purpose: To state how [AGENCY NAME] uses nursing services, when a nurse consultant is used, and how nursing tasks and medication tasks are limited to appropriately licensed or authorized staff.
policies.policy: Nursing tasks are performed only by licensed nurses, and only a licensed nurse may delegate a nursing task. Each staff member works only within the tasks for which the person is licensed, trained and authorized. [AGENCY NAME] uses a nurse consultant, with the hours set by the Administrator based on the residents' needs; these hours are an operator choice and not a minimum set by rule. Under 10A NCAC 13F .1004, medications are administered only by staff who meet 10A NCAC 13F .0403 and G.S. 131D-4.5B: staff who give or prepare medications, and their direct supervisors, must complete the required training and clinical skills validation and pass the written exam. Persons whose occupational licensure law authorizes them to administer medications (for example, licensed nurses) are exempt from the medication aide training. Details of medication practice are in MED-01 and MED-02.

definitions.definition: A licensed nurse engaged by the facility to assess, advise, teach and review care. The number of hours is set by the Administrator.
A licensed nurse's transfer of a nursing task to another person who has been trained and found competent, with the nurse remaining accountable for the delegation decision.
A staff member who has completed the training and skills validation and passed the written exam, and who may administer medications under 10A NCAC 13F .0403.
A person, such as a licensed nurse, whose licensing law permits the administration of medications.
The facility's written confirmation of the tasks a staff member is trained and permitted to perform (see MED-01).

procedures: The Administrator decides which nursing needs residents have, based on assessments (ADM-02), care plans (ADM-03) and physician orders, and decides whether to use a nurse consultant, an employed nurse, or both. The decision and hours are written in the staffing plan [NURSE CONSULTANT NAME / HOURS].
The Administrator verifies each nurse's license in the NC Board of Nursing license look-up before the first day of work and each year after that, and keeps a copy in the personnel file (STF-02).

The nurse consultant performs the tasks assigned by the Administrator, such as reviewing residents with changes of condition, teaching staff, reviewing care plans and checking medication practices. The nurse writes a dated note of each visit.
The Administrator keeps a written list of nursing tasks performed in the facility and who is allowed to perform them. Tasks outside a person's license, training or authorization are not assigned.

Only a licensed nurse delegates a nursing task. The nurse trains the staff member, checks and documents competence, tells the staff member exactly what is to be done and when to report, and checks the care afterward. The delegation is recorded in the personnel file and the resident's record.
Aides and other unlicensed staff do not do assessments, make nursing judgments or perform nursing tasks that have not been delegated to them by a licensed nurse.

Before a staff member is allowed to give or prepare any medication, the Administrator verifies that the staff member either is authorized by occupational licensure or has completed the required medication aide training and clinical skills validation and passed the written exam. The Administrator also verifies that the supervisor of such staff has met the same requirements (C6). Proof is placed in the personnel file (STF-02, MED-01).
Medications are administered only on the order of a licensed prescriber, and the MAR is charted immediately after each administration, as set out in MED-01. Pre-charting is not allowed.

Staff who are unsure whether a task is within their authority stop and ask the nurse or Administrator before doing it. Staff report any concern or error to the Administrator at once. Medication errors are handled under MED-02.

The Administrator reviews task assignments and nurse consultant notes at least quarterly and makes changes in hours or duties as residents' needs change. The review is brought to the quality meeting (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Decides on nursing coverage and consultant hours, verifies licenses and authorization, and keeps staff within their scope.
Performs nursing tasks, delegates only after training and competence checks, and documents visits and delegations.
Administer medications only within their authorization and report errors and concerns.
Perform only tasks they are trained and authorized to perform.

documentation: Nurse consultant agreement and visit notes
Nursing license verification records
Written delegation records and competency checks
Medication aide training, skills validation and exam records
List of nursing tasks and authorized staff

policies.title: Change of Condition, Physician Notification and Hospital Transfer
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Home (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Home (10A NCAC 13G)
policies.purpose: To make sure that a resident's change of condition is recognized quickly, the physician and responsible person are told promptly, the resident is reassessed and the care plan updated, and a resident who is sent to the hospital goes with the information the receiving provider needs.
policies.policy: Staff report any change in a resident's physical, mental or functional condition to the Administrator or manager right away. The facility notifies the resident's physician (or other prescriber) and the responsible person promptly and documents the notification. A significant change in condition triggers a reassessment under 10A NCAC 13F .0801, in addition to the assessment within 30 days of admission and each year, and a prompt update of the care plan (ADM-02, ADM-03). In an emergency, staff call 911 first. When a resident is transferred to a hospital, the facility sends the medication list, the current MAR, the face sheet and the advance directive, if any. Any incident is also handled under INC-01.

definitions.definition: Any new or worsening sign, symptom, behavior, function or need, such as a fall, injury, new confusion, loss of appetite, new pain or changes in skin, vital signs, mobility or mood.
A change in condition that is major, is not expected to resolve quickly, or affects more than one area of function, and that requires a new assessment and care plan revision.
A one-page summary of the resident's identifying information, emergency contacts, responsible person, physician, diagnoses, allergies and insurance.
The family member, friend or other person designated in the resident's record to be notified, as defined in 10A NCAC 13F .0102.

procedures: Any staff member who notices a change in condition tells the Administrator, manager or nurse on duty immediately. Staff do not wait until the end of the shift for urgent changes.

In a life-threatening emergency (unresponsive, not breathing, chest pain, stroke signs, severe bleeding, serious injury), staff call 911 first, begin first aid or CPR as trained, and then notify the Administrator.
For non-emergency changes, the manager or nurse checks the resident, records vital signs if ordered or appropriate, and decides if the physician needs to be called now or if an appointment is needed.

The responsible staff member calls the physician or prescriber and gives the resident's name, the change, when it began, current medications and allergies, and writes down the instructions and the name of the person who gave them. Orders are written and followed under MED-01.

The same staff member promptly notifies the responsible person and the legal representative, if different, of the change and the physician's instructions. The date, time, person reached and content of the call are documented. If no one can be reached, the attempts are recorded.
The staff member writes a dated and timed note in the resident's record that describes the change, the actions taken, who was notified and the resident's response.

If the change may be a significant change, the Administrator arranges a reassessment under 10A NCAC 13F .0801 by a person who meets the assessor requirements (ADM-02), and updates the care plan with the resident and responsible person (ADM-03). The update is made within a time that matches the resident's needs and no later than when the new assessment is complete.
Staff increase supervision and checks as the physician orders or the situation requires, and communicate this to the next shift in the shift report.

When a resident is transferred to the hospital, a staff member prepares a packet with the current medication list, a copy of the MAR, the face sheet and the advance directive or DNR order, if one exists (RR-03). The packet goes with the resident or is sent immediately.

A staff member goes with the resident or follows when staffing allows, or phones the hospital with the information that staff know about the resident, and provides the responsible person with the hospital's name.

The Administrator contacts the hospital within [24 hours] to confirm the resident's status and to plan return. On return, the Administrator or nurse reviews discharge instructions and new orders with the physician or pharmacy, updates the MAR and care plan, and decides if the facility can meet the resident's needs (ADM-04).
The Administrator completes and files any incident report and required notifications for injuries, falls or other incidents that led to the change (INC-01, REC-02).
The Administrator reviews changes of condition and hospital transfers at the quality meeting to look for trends (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Notice and report changes immediately, call 911 in an emergency and document what they observe.
Evaluate the resident, notify the physician and responsible person, and prepare the transfer packet.
Makes sure reassessment and care plan updates are completed, follows up with the hospital, completes reports and reviews trends.
Gives orders and instructions for the resident's care.

documentation: Dated and timed progress note of the change and actions taken
Physician notification and orders record
Responsible person notification record
Reassessment and updated care plan
Transfer packet checklist (medication list, MAR, face sheet, advance directive)
Incident report, if applicable

policies.title: Dementia and Memory Care (Special Care Unit)
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Home (10A NCAC 13F), including any Alzheimer's/dementia special care unit; Family Care Home (10A NCAC 13G) for residents who are disoriented or wander
policies.purpose: To describe how [AGENCY NAME] cares for residents with Alzheimer's disease and other dementias, including how a special care unit is operated and reported, and the supervision required for residents who are disoriented or who wander.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides care for residents with dementia that is based on each resident's assessment and care plan, and that protects the resident's safety, dignity and quality of life. If the facility operates a special care unit, it follows the Division's special care unit requirements for the resident profile, care plan, staffing and disclosure, and it lists the special care unit beds on the annual renewal application (10A NCAC 13F .0208) along with bed capacity and census data. In a facility with 7 to 12 residents, an awake staff member is on duty at all times if any resident is disoriented or wanders (staffing rules effective 9/1/2024). Staffing for larger facilities and for special care units follows STF-01. Wandering and door alarms are managed under WAN-01, missing residents under MIS-01 and restraints under RST-01. For information only: the 2026 State/County Special Assistance rate for a special care unit resident is $1,792 per month. The facility explains charges and what is included to families as stated in the resident contract (CON-01).

definitions.definition: A designated part of the facility, with its own beds, staff and program, that serves residents with Alzheimer's disease or other dementias.
A resident who is confused about person, place or time such that the resident cannot safely look after themselves without supervision.
Moving about without a clear purpose or awareness of safety, including leaving the building or grounds without staff knowing.
A staff member who is awake and available to residents and able to respond immediately, including during the night shift (11:01 p.m. to 7:00 a.m.).
A written description of the type of resident the unit serves, including the care needs and behaviors the unit can and cannot manage.

procedures: At pre-admission screening (ADM-01), the Administrator or designee asks about memory loss, disorientation, wandering, exit-seeking and behaviors. The Administrator decides whether the facility, or its special care unit, can safely meet the person's needs (ADM-04).
At admission and at each reassessment (ADM-02), the assessor records the resident's cognitive status, behavior, wandering risk and need for supervision.

The care plan (ADM-03) for each resident with dementia includes the resident's routines and preferences, the level of supervision, communication approaches, ways to prevent and respond to agitation without restraints (RST-01), safety needs, meaningful activities (ACT-01) and family involvement.

If the facility has a special care unit, the Administrator keeps a written description of the unit (resident profile, admission and discharge criteria, program, staffing, safety features) and gives it to prospective residents and families before admission. The unit's care plans meet the Division's special care unit requirements.
The Administrator keeps current the list of beds in the special care unit and reports them on the annual renewal application with capacity and census (GOV-02).

In a 7-12 resident facility, the manager schedules an awake staff member at all times, including 3rd shift, whenever any resident is disoriented or wanders. The schedule shows the name of the awake staff member for each shift (STF-01).

Staff caring for residents with dementia complete orientation and ongoing training on dementia care, communication, behaviors and wandering and exit-seeking prevention before they work independently and each year after that (STF-03). The Administrator keeps the training records.

Staff identify residents at risk of wandering and follow WAN-01: current photo and description, regular checks, door alarms tested and working. A resident who cannot be found is handled under MIS-01 at once.

Staff respond to distress and behaviors by looking for causes (pain, hunger, toileting, noise, change in routine), redirecting calmly and using the alternatives in RST-01. Behaviors that are new or worse are reported under HLT-03.
Staff offer daily structured activities that match each resident's abilities and interests, and include some activities in the evening and on weekends.
The manager checks each shift that the unit environment is safe: hazards removed, exits secured as the fire code permits (FIR-01), and residents can walk safely.
The Administrator reviews the unit's census, incidents, falls, elopement attempts and staffing at least quarterly and takes the results to the quality meeting (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Decides who can be safely served, sets up and describes the special care unit, reports unit beds on renewal, makes sure awake staffing and training are in place.
Schedules awake staff, supervises care and checks the environment each shift.
Carry out the care plan, supervise residents at risk of wandering, use non-restraint approaches and report changes and missing residents at once.
Plan and lead activities that are suited to residents with dementia.

documentation: Pre-admission screening and assessment records showing cognitive status and wandering risk
Care plans with dementia-specific interventions
Written special care unit description and resident profile (if applicable)
Renewal application listing special care unit beds
Staff schedules showing awake staff on all shifts, as required
Dementia training records
Quarterly review of incidents and elopement attempts

policies.title: Falls Prevention
policies.applies_to: Adult Care Home (10A NCAC 13F) and Family Care Home (10A NCAC 13G); all residents, all staff
policies.purpose: To reduce the number and severity of resident falls by identifying fall risk early, putting individualized prevention measures into the care plan, responding correctly when a fall occurs, and learning from every fall.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] assesses every resident's fall risk at admission, at least annually, and after any fall. Fall risk is considered as part of the functional resident assessment required by 10A NCAC 13F .0801 (within 30 days of admission, annually, and after a significant change of condition). Fall-prevention interventions are written into the resident-centered care plan required by 10A NCAC 13F .0802, include the resident's preferences, and are kept where staff can access them. The care plan is reviewed after each fall. Falls with injury are reported according to INC-01. [AGENCY NAME] does not use physical restraints or bed rails as a fall-prevention measure; see RST-01. The reference to 13F rules applies equally to the equivalent 13G assessment and care-planning requirements in a Family Care Home.

definitions.definition: An unplanned descent to the floor or other lower surface, whether or not the resident is injured and whether or not the fall was witnessed.
A fall that results in any injury requiring first aid beyond routine cleaning of a minor mark, or any medical evaluation, treatment or hospital transfer.
A short facility-approved checklist ([FALL RISK TOOL]) covering fall history, gait and balance, mobility devices, medications, vision, cognition, continence and footwear.
A major change in a resident's physical, cognitive, mood or functional status that triggers reassessment under the assessment rule.

procedures: During pre-admission screening (ADM-01), the Administrator or designee asks about falls in the past 12 months, mobility devices, dizziness, vision, and medications, and records the answers on the screening form.

On the day of admission, the designated staff member completes the fall-risk screen with the resident and responsible person and records the result in the resident record. Residents who score at risk are flagged on the care plan.

The qualified assessor completes the DHSR assessment instrument (or an approved equivalent) within 30 days of admission under 10A NCAC 13F .0801, and reviews mobility, balance, cognition, medications, continence and vision as they relate to fall risk.
The Administrator or designee repeats the fall-risk screen at least annually with the annual assessment, and whenever there is a significant change of condition.

The care plan (ADM-03; 10A NCAC 13F .0802) lists each resident's specific interventions, such as assistance level for transfers and walking, mobility device, toileting schedule, footwear, call or check frequency, and the resident's stated preferences. A current copy is kept where all staff can read it.
Staff review the care plan before providing care, and use only the assistance and devices listed for that resident.

Staff walk the building each shift to check for clutter, spills, poor lighting, loose rugs, cords, and unsafe furniture placement, and correct hazards immediately. Hazards that cannot be fixed right away are reported to the Administrator the same day (DLV-01).

The Administrator asks the resident's physician or pharmacist to review medications that may increase fall risk when a resident has repeated falls or a new at-risk medication is started (MED-01, MED-02).

Residents who are disoriented or at risk of wandering are supervised according to WAN-01. Restraints and bed rails are not used to prevent falls (RST-01); alternatives such as low beds, bed/chair alarms where appropriate, and scheduled toileting are tried first.
